comments.text:
Companion HTML explainer for the current Workbench body of work. Captured before Task 1 delivery, with active and pending status explicit. It supplements the canonical specification and plan without replacing either. Local path: .dev/design/morphir-workbench-explainer.html Document title

Morphir Workbench: what the work enables

Maintainer orientation · 17 October 2026 · delivered foundation, active implementation, future policy

The Workbench turns source projects or saved Morphir models into something a person can inspect and evaluate. The browser and Proton desktop application share the interface and model pipeline. Their adapters decide where work runs and which capabilities the current host actually offers.

The native/client/owner foundation is delivered. Permissive typed admission is a new feature being implemented, beginning with morphir-etg2.16.1. The approved design is complete; no permissive runtime capability is shipped or advertised yet.

  • One interface, different execution hosts
  • Two concrete workflows
  • Why typed admission and outcomes exist
  • Snapshots, jobs and revocation
  • Why the independent MCK matters
  • What is done and what is current
  • What permissive will mean
  • Six implementation phases
  • Evidence and scope

One interface, different execution hosts

ExperienceWhere work runsBoundary that matters
Standalone browserA local Web Worker runs compilation, import, inspection and supported evaluation.Selected files are data supplied to the worker. They do not grant general access to the user's filesystem.
Proton desktopThe same UI uses a bundled, page-bound native adapter. Local compilation remains available; offered native workspace and typed jobs go through the native Owner and its services.The native host supplies caller identity, the directory picker and worker executable. Renderer data cannot create that authority.
Connected modeAn authenticated adapter uses the host's advertised compile, generate and workspace methods. A separately offered jobs extension can select a job-enabled gateway/provider.The real Rust connected-v1 acceptance has jobs:false. A connected session alone does not enable evaluation or cancellation.

Source frontends produce Morphir IR, the common model representation. Model Explorer reads that model; generators produce target artifacts; an evaluator runs a selected function. These are separate steps. A successful import, an inspectable model or generated code does not by itself prove a function can run in a particular evaluator.

Two concrete workflows

One interface, different execution hosts

Standalone browserA local Web Worker runs compilation, import, inspection and supported evaluation.Selected files are data supplied to the worker. They do not grant general access to the user's filesystem.

Source frontends produce Morphir IR, the common model representation. Model Explorer reads that model; generators produce target artifacts; an evaluator runs a selected function. These are separate steps. A successful import, an inspectable model or generated code does not by itself prove a function can run in a particular evaluator.

Two concrete workflows

Edit a project, inspect its model, evaluate a function

  1. Open or create a source project, edit its files, and compile through the selected frontend.
  2. Inspect accepted IR in Model Explorer and view generated artifacts or generation diagnostics. The model can remain inspectable when a later generation step fails.
  3. Select an available public function and enter typed arguments through fields, tagged JSON or Ion text.
  4. Evaluate using an available runtime. Read the typed result or terminal diagnostic in the results panel. Later edits and stale replies cannot replace the current view with an obsolete result.

The Workbench's surfaced typed evaluation still uses the strict checking policy. Dynamic Scheme and worksheet evaluation are separate experiences; they are not a shortcut around typed boundary validation.

Open a native workspace and run an owned job

  1. The bundled Proton page opens a native session. Offered workspace access lets the host ask the user to choose a directory and return scoped project references.
  2. Opening a saved model captures its original bytes. Bounded chunk reads use the retained capture, rather than silently switching to a later file or model.
  3. Typed submission captures the model, public entry, arguments and provider into one immutable job snapshot. A worker claims that job once.
  4. Query observes submitted, running or terminal receipts. Cancel requests termination; the terminal receipt follows the execution and cleanup result. A completed result may win the cancellation race.
  5. Release retires retained terminal evidence. Navigation, renderer failure, page replacement or shutdown revokes the old session and closes its owned resources.

Browser folder upload, CEF selected-file replay and a native workspace grant are different mechanisms. The packaged smoke exercises the normal selected-file reader/import/compiler, but it does not qualify choosing a folder in the operating-system dialog.

Runtime capabilities, verification and validation

Runtime capabilities describe what a runtime supports: model versions, execution modes, operations, types and resource limits. A model can describe more than a chosen runtime supports, so a capability claim needs evidence and each run needs its own compatibility checks.

Capability verification gathers scoped evidence that a runtime behaves as claimed through versioned contracts and the shared MCK. It is not formal proof, a guarantee for every program, or a claim that business logic is correct.

A selected function with a function-valued argument still fails capability validation when that boundary is unsupported. Even a compatible call needs valid arguments, and its actual returned value needs output validation.

Validation of what actually came back prevents a plausible-looking value or malformed reply from becoming a successful typed result.

A snapshot fixes what a job will execute. Editing the source, changing arguments, switching projects or reconnecting cannot rewrite an accepted job. Job and snapshot identities remain bound to their host, session and provider. Query does not execute again, and a terminal result is immutable.

Cancellation acknowledgement is an intermediate fact. Different evidence proves different things. Codec suites verify handling of values within their stated contracts; each actual value is still validated. Client suites verify scoped boundary behavior. Morphir Workbench: what the work enables

Maintainer orientation · 17 October 2026 · delivered foundation and two internal slices; Task 3 locally qualified, paired merges pending

The Workbench turns source projects or saved Morphir models into something a person can inspect and evaluate. The browser and Proton desktop application share the interface and model pipeline. Their adapters decide where work runs and which capabilities the current host actually offers.

The native/client/owner foundation and Tasks 16.1 and 16.2 are delivered. Task 16.3 immutable Scheme jobs is locally qualified and awaiting paired merges. Merged progress remains 2 of 6 tasks, 33.3%, with 4 remaining. Public UI and existing native/HTTP offers remain strict; Task 4 standalone controls is next.

  • One interface, different execution hosts
  • Two concrete workflows
  • Runtime capabilities, verification and validation
  • Snapshots, jobs and revocation
  • Why the independent MCK matters
  • What is done and what is current
  • Checking policy for unsupported code
  • Six implementation phases
  • Evidence and scope

One interface, different execution hosts

ExperienceWhere work runsBoundary that matters
Standalone browserA local Web Worker runs compilation, import, inspection and supported evaluation.Selected files are data supplied to the worker. They do not grant general access to the user's filesystem.
Proton desktopThe same UI uses a bundled, page-bound native adapter. Local compilation remains available; offered native workspace and typed jobs go through the native Owner and its services.The native host supplies caller identity, the directory picker and worker executable. Renderer data cannot create that authority.
Connected modeAn authenticated adapter uses the host's advertised compile, generate and workspace methods. A separately offered jobs extension can select a job-enabled gateway/provider.The real Rust connected-v1 acceptance has jobs:false. A connected session alone does not enable evaluation or cancellation.

Source frontends produce Morphir IR, the common model representation. Model Explorer reads that model; generators produce target artifacts; an evaluator runs a selected function. These are separate steps. A successful import, an inspectable model or generated code does not by itself prove a function can run in a particular evaluator.

Two concrete workflows

Edit a project, inspect its model, evaluate a function

  1. Open or create a source project, edit its files, and compile through the selected frontend.
  2. Inspect accepted IR in Model Explorer and view generated artifacts or generation diagnostics. The model can remain inspectable when a later generation step fails.
  3. Select an available public function and enter typed arguments through fields, tagged JSON or Ion text.
  4. Evaluate using an available runtime. Read the typed result or terminal diagnostic in the results panel. Later edits and stale replies cannot replace the current view with an obsolete result.

The Workbench's surfaced typed evaluation still uses the strict checking policy. Dynamic Scheme and worksheet evaluation are separate experiences; they are not a shortcut around typed boundary validation.

Open a native workspace and run an owned job

  1. The bundled Proton page opens a native session. Offered workspace access lets the host ask the user to choose a directory and return scoped project references.
  2. Opening a saved model captures its original bytes. Bounded chunk reads use the retained capture, rather than silently switching to a later file or model.
  3. Typed submission captures the model, public entry, arguments and provider into one immutable job snapshot. A worker claims that job once.
  4. Query observes submitted, running or terminal receipts. Cancel requests termination; the terminal receipt follows the execution and cleanup result. A completed result may win the cancellation race.
  5. Release retires retained terminal evidence. Navigation, renderer failure, page replacement or shutdown revokes the old session and closes its owned resources.

Browser folder upload, CEF selected-file replay and a native workspace grant are different mechanisms. The packaged smoke exercises the normal selected-file reader/import/compiler, but it does not qualify choosing a folder in the operating-system dialog.

Runtime capabilities, verification and validation

Runtime capabilities describe what a runtime supports: model versions, execution modes, operations, types and resource limits. A model can describe more than a chosen runtime supports, so a capability claim needs evidence and each run needs its own compatibility checks.

Capability verification gathers scoped evidence that a runtime behaves as claimed through versioned contracts and the shared MCK. It is not formal proof, a guarantee for every program, or a claim that business logic is correct.

ActivityQuestion it answersConcrete example
Capability verificationDoes this runtime behave as claimed within the tested contract and scope?Fixed independent cases exercise the Library-only selected Scheme planner and check its results and refusals.
Capability validationDo this selected function and model revision fit the chosen runtime's capabilities for this run?Match its public signature, complete selected types and checking policy to the runtime's support.

For example, verified bounded integer support does not make every function in the model runnable. A selected function with a function-valued argument still fails capability validation when that boundary is unsupported. Even a compatible call needs valid arguments, and its actual returned value needs output validation.

Data, models, types, arguments, outputs, receipts and authority remain subject to validation. Validate source integrity, public visibility, exact arity, complete custom types and resource bounds. Validation of what actually came back prevents a plausible-looking value or malformed reply from becoming a successful typed result.

EvidenceMeaning
Returned valueOrdinary typed data. A typed Result.Err is still returned data, not an infrastructure failure.
SDK model errorOne of the enumerated semantic errors, such as division by zero. It has its own model-error outcome.
Primary failurePlanning, provider, build, invocation or evaluation failed. It must retain its stage and diagnostic.
CancelledTerminal cancellation evidence, distinct from merely acknowledging a cancel request.
Cleanup failureSeparate evidence that can accompany any terminal result. It does not overwrite the primary cause or returned value.

Snapshots, jobs and revocation

A snapshot fixes what a job will execute. Editing the source, changing arguments, switching projects or reconnecting cannot rewrite an accepted job. Job and snapshot identities remain bound to their host, session and provider. Query does not execute again, and a terminal result is immutable.

Cancellation acknowledgement is an intermediate fact. A timeout or lost connection can leave work running, so the client retains its last receipt and avoids inventing failure, cancellation or safe-to-retry submission. The native host confirms worker exit and cleanup separately. A new page cannot borrow an old page's session or workspace grant.

The locally qualified Task 16.3 private Scheme job path captures the original source, ordered calls and arguments, complete selected boundary, runtime, provider and effective policy. A once-only claim gives the actual worker that retained selection. Replanning copies retained inputs into a new job, snapshot and plan identity; original jobs remain independent. Changing caller data or a later default cannot rewrite accepted work.

The first worker-plan mismatch stays a failure; a later matching message cannot clear it. Actual isolated Node worker tests cover this boundary separately from controlled in-memory traces. Surfaced UI controls and native/HTTP capability offers remain pending integrations.

The shared Rust Morphir Compatibility Kit owns the fixed cases, expected observations and compatibility verdicts. An explicit implementation adapter receives inputs, drives production behavior and returns observations. It receives neither expected results nor case IDs. The Rust checker reloads the exact corpus and recomputes qualification from the saved report.

This separates a requirement from the implementation being tested. A second verdict engine inside the Workbench would let both sides share the same mistaken assumptions.

Different evidence proves different things. Codec suites verify handling of values within their stated contracts; each actual value is still validated. Client suites verify scoped boundary behavior. The 43-trace Owner suite drives actual Owner, Session and Workspace policy with controlled jobs Host and memory IO. Real worker exit, filesystem containment, authenticated connections and packaged acceptance use separate tests. Controlled completions do not establish real OS provenance or worker execution.

One interface, different execution hosts

ExperienceWhere work runsBoundary that matters

Source frontends produce Morphir IR, the common model representation. Model Explorer reads that model; generators produce target artifacts; an evaluator runs a selected function. These are separate steps. A successful import, an inspectable model or generated code does not by itself prove a function can run in a particular evaluator.

Two concrete workflows

Edit a project, inspect its model, evaluate a function

  1. Open or create a source project, edit its files, and compile through the selected frontend.
  2. Inspect accepted IR in Model Explorer and view generated artifacts or generation diagnostics. The model can remain inspectable when a later generation step fails.
  3. Select an available public function and enter typed arguments through fields, tagged JSON or Ion text.
  4. Evaluate using an available runtime. Read the typed result or terminal diagnostic in the results panel. Later edits and stale replies cannot replace the current view with an obsolete result.

The Workbench's surfaced typed evaluation still uses the strict checking policy. Dynamic Scheme and worksheet evaluation are separate experiences; they are not a shortcut around typed boundary validation.

  1. The bundled Proton page opens a native session. Offered workspace access lets the host ask the user to choose a directory and return scoped project references.

  3. Typed submission captures the model, public entry, arguments and provider into one immutable job snapshot. A worker claims that job once.
  4. Query observes submitted, running or terminal receipts. Cancel requests termination; the terminal receipt follows the execution and cleanup result. A completed result may win the cancellation race.
  5. Release retires retained terminal evidence. Navigation, renderer failure, page replacement or shutdown revokes the old session and closes its owned resources.

Browser folder upload, CEF selected-file replay and a native workspace grant are different mechanisms. The packaged smoke exercises the normal selected-file reader/import/compiler, but it does not qualify choosing a folder in the operating-system dialog.

Runtime capabilities describe what a runtime supports: model versions, execution modes, operations, types and resource limits. A model can describe more than a chosen runtime supports, so a capability claim needs evidence and each run needs its own compatibility checks.

Capability verification gathers scoped evidence that a runtime behaves as claimed through versioned contracts and the shared MCK. It is not formal proof, a guarantee for every program, or a claim that business logic is correct.

ActivityQuestion it answersConcrete example

Capability validationDo this selected function and model revision fit the chosen runtime's capabilities for this run?Match its public signature, complete selected types and checking policy to the runtime's support.

For example, verified bounded integer support does not make every function in the model runnable. A selected function with a function-valued argument still fails capability validation when that boundary is unsupported. Even a compatible call needs valid arguments, and its actual returned value needs output validation.

Data, models, types, arguments, outputs, receipts and authority remain subject to validation. Validate source integrity, public visibility, exact arity, complete custom types and resource bounds. Returned valueOrdinary typed data. A typed Result.Err is still returned data, not an infrastructure failure.

Primary failurePlanning, provider, build, invocation or evaluation failed. It must retain its stage and diagnostic.

A snapshot fixes what a job will execute. Editing the source, changing arguments, switching projects or reconnecting cannot rewrite an accepted job. Job and snapshot identities remain bound to their host, session and provider. Query does not execute again, and a terminal result is immutable.

Cancellation acknowledgement is an intermediate fact. A timeout or lost connection can leave work running, so the client retains its last receipt and avoids inventing failure, cancellation or safe-to-retry submission. The native host confirms worker exit and cleanup separately. A new page cannot borrow an old page's session or workspace grant.

A once-only claim gives the actual worker that retained selection. Replanning copies retained inputs into a new job, snapshot and plan identity; original jobs remain independent. Changing caller data or a later default cannot rewrite accepted work.

  1. Open or create a source project, edit its files, and compile through the selected frontend.
  2. Inspect accepted IR in Model Explorer and view generated artifacts or generation diagnostics. The model can remain inspectable when a later generation step fails.
  3. Select an available public function and enter typed arguments through fields, tagged JSON or Ion text.
  4. Evaluate using an available runtime. Read the typed result or terminal diagnostic in the results panel. Later edits and stale replies cannot replace the current view with an obsolete result.

The Workbench's surfaced typed evaluation still uses the strict checking policy. Dynamic Scheme and worksheet evaluation are separate experiences; they are not a shortcut around typed boundary validation.

Open a native workspace and run an owned job

  1. The bundled Proton page opens a native session. Offered workspace access lets the host ask the user to choose a directory and return scoped project references.
  2. Opening a saved model captures its original bytes. Bounded chunk reads use the retained capture, rather than silently switching to a later file or model.
  3. Typed submission captures the model, public entry, arguments and provider into one immutable job snapshot. A worker claims that job once.
  4. Query observes submitted, running or terminal receipts. Cancel requests termination; the terminal receipt follows the execution and cleanup result. A completed result may win the cancellation race.
  5. Release retires retained terminal evidence. Navigation, renderer failure, page replacement or shutdown revokes the old session and closes its owned resources.

Browser folder upload, CEF selected-file replay and a native workspace grant are different mechanisms. The packaged smoke exercises the normal selected-file reader/import/compiler, but it does not qualify choosing a folder in the operating-system dialog.

Runtime capabilities, verification and validation

Runtime capabilities describe what a runtime supports: model versions, execution modes, operations, types and resource limits. A model can describe more than a chosen runtime supports, so a capability claim needs evidence and each run needs its own compatibility checks.

Capability verification gathers scoped evidence that a runtime behaves as claimed through versioned contracts and the shared MCK. It is not formal proof, a guarantee for every program, or a claim that business logic is correct.

ActivityQuestion it answersConcrete example
Capability verificationDoes this runtime behave as claimed within the tested contract and scope?Fixed independent cases exercise the Library-only selected Scheme planner and check its results and refusals.
Capability validationDo this selected function and model revision fit the chosen runtime's capabilities for this run?Match its public signature, complete selected types and checking policy to the runtime's support.

For example, verified bounded integer support does not make every function in the model runnable. A selected function with a function-valued argument still fails capability validation when that boundary is unsupported. Even a compatible call needs valid arguments, and its actual returned value needs output validation.

Data, models, types, arguments, outputs, receipts and authority remain subject to validation. Validate source integrity, public visibility, exact arity, complete custom types and resource bounds. Validation of what actually came back prevents a plausible-looking value or malformed reply from becoming a successful typed result.

EvidenceMeaning
Returned valueOrdinary typed data. A typed Result.Err is still returned data, not an infrastructure failure.
SDK model errorOne of the enumerated semantic errors, such as division by zero. It has its own model-error outcome.
Primary failurePlanning, provider, build, invocation or evaluation failed. It must retain its stage and diagnostic.
CancelledTerminal cancellation evidence, distinct from merely acknowledging a cancel request.
Cleanup failureSeparate evidence that can accompany any terminal result. It does not overwrite the primary cause or returned value.

Snapshots, jobs and revocation

A snapshot fixes what a job will execute. Editing the source, changing arguments, switching projects or reconnecting cannot rewrite an accepted job. Job and snapshot identities remain bound to their host, session and provider. Query does not execute again, and a terminal result is immutable.

Cancellation acknowledgement is an intermediate fact. A timeout or lost connection can leave work running, so the client retains its last receipt and avoids inventing failure, cancellation or safe-to-retry submission. The native host confirms worker exit and cleanup separately. A new page cannot borrow an old page's session or workspace grant.

The locally qualified Task 16.3 private Scheme job path captures the original source, ordered calls and arguments, complete selected boundary, runtime, provider and effective policy. A once-only claim gives the actual worker that retained selection. Replanning copies retained inputs into a new job, snapshot and plan identity; original jobs remain independent. Changing caller data or a later default cannot rewrite accepted work.

The first worker-plan mismatch stays a failure; a later matching message cannot clear it. Actual isolated Node worker tests cover this boundary separately from controlled in-memory traces. Surfaced UI controls and native/HTTP capability offers remain pending integrations.

Why the independent MCK matters

The shared Rust Morphir Compatibility Kit owns the fixed cases, expected observations and compatibility verdicts. An explicit implementation adapter receives inputs, drives production behavior and returns observations. It receives neither expected results nor case IDs. The Rust checker reloads the exact corpus and recomputes qualification from the saved report.

This separates a requirement from the implementation being tested. A second verdict engine inside the Workbench would let both sides share the same mistaken assumptions.

Different evidence proves different things. Codec suites verify handling of values within their stated contracts; each actual value is still validated. Client suites verify scoped boundary behavior. The 43-trace Owner suite drives actual Owner, Session and Workspace policy with controlled jobs Host and memory IO. Real worker exit, filesystem containment, authenticated connections and packaged acceptance use separate tests. Controlled completions do not establish real OS provenance or worker execution.

Maintainer orientation · 17 October 2026 · delivered foundation and three internal slices; standalone controls in progress

The Workbench turns source projects or saved Morphir models into something a person can inspect and evaluate. The browser and Proton desktop application share the interface and model pipeline. Their adapters decide where work runs and which capabilities the current host actually offers.

The native/client/owner foundation and Tasks 16.1 through 16.3 are delivered. Merged progress is 3 of 6 tasks, 50%, with 3 remaining. Task 4 standalone controls is in progress; qualification and delivery remain pending. Public UI and existing native/HTTP offers remain strict.

  • One interface, different execution hosts

  • Snapshots, jobs and revocation
  • Why the independent MCK matters
  • What is done and what is current
  • Checking policy for unsupported code
  • Six implementation phases
  • Evidence and scope

One interface, different execution hosts

ExperienceWhere work runsBoundary that matters
Standalone browserA local Web Worker runs compilation, import, inspection and supported evaluation.Selected files are data supplied to the worker. They do not grant general access to the user's filesystem.
Proton desktopThe same UI uses a bundled, page-bound native adapter. Local compilation remains available; offered native workspace and typed jobs go through the native Owner and its services.The native host supplies caller identity, the directory picker and worker executable. Renderer data cannot create that authority.
Connected modeAn authenticated adapter uses the host's advertised compile, generate and workspace methods. A separately offered jobs extension can select a job-enabled gateway/provider.The real Rust connected-v1 acceptance has jobs:false. A connected session alone does not enable evaluation or cancellation.

Source frontends produce Morphir IR, the common model representation. Model Explorer reads that model; generators produce target artifacts; an evaluator runs a selected function. These are separate steps. A successful import, an inspectable model or generated code does not by itself prove a function can run in a particular evaluator.

Two concrete workflows

Edit a project, inspect its model, evaluate a function

  1. Open or create a source project, edit its files, and compile through the selected frontend.
  2. Inspect accepted IR in Model Explorer and view generated artifacts or generation diagnostics. The model can remain inspectable when a later generation step fails.
  3. Select an available public function and enter typed arguments through fields, tagged JSON or Ion text.
  4. Evaluate using an available runtime. Read the typed result or terminal diagnostic in the results panel. Later edits and stale replies cannot replace the current view with an obsolete result.

The Workbench's surfaced typed evaluation still uses the strict checking policy. Dynamic Scheme and worksheet evaluation are separate experiences; they are not a shortcut around typed boundary validation.

Open a native workspace and run an owned job

  1. The bundled Proton page opens a native session. Offered workspace access lets the host ask the user to choose a directory and return scoped project references.
  2. Opening a saved model captures its original bytes. Bounded chunk reads use the retained capture, rather than silently switching to a later file or model.
  3. Typed submission captures the model, public entry, arguments and provider into one immutable job snapshot. A worker claims that job once.
  4. Query observes submitted, running or terminal receipts. Cancel requests termination; the terminal receipt follows the execution and cleanup result. A completed result may win the cancellation race.
  5. Release retires retained terminal evidence. Navigation, renderer failure, page replacement or shutdown revokes the old session and closes its owned resources.

Browser folder upload, CEF selected-file replay and a native workspace grant are different mechanisms. The packaged smoke exercises the normal selected-file reader/import/compiler, but it does not qualify choosing a folder in the operating-system dialog.

Runtime capabilities, verification and validation

Runtime capabilities describe what a runtime supports: model versions, execution modes, operations, types and resource limits. A model can describe more than a chosen runtime supports, so a capability claim needs evidence and each run needs its own compatibility checks.

Capability verification gathers scoped evidence that a runtime behaves as claimed through versioned contracts and the shared MCK. It is not formal proof, a guarantee for every program, or a claim that business logic is correct.

ActivityQuestion it answersConcrete example
Capability verificationDoes this runtime behave as claimed within the tested contract and scope?Fixed independent cases exercise the Library-only selected Scheme planner and check its results and refusals.
Capability validationDo this selected function and model revision fit the chosen runtime's capabilities for this run?Match its public signature, complete selected types and checking policy to the runtime's support.

For example, verified bounded integer support does not make every function in the model runnable. A selected function with a function-valued argument still fails capability validation when that boundary is unsupported. Even a compatible call needs valid arguments, and its actual returned value needs output validation.

Data, models, types, arguments, outputs, receipts and authority remain subject to validation. Validate source integrity, public visibility, exact arity, complete custom types and resource bounds. Validation of what actually came back prevents a plausible-looking value or malformed reply from becoming a successful typed result.

EvidenceMeaning
Returned valueOrdinary typed data. A typed Result.Err is still returned data, not an infrastructure failure.
SDK model errorOne of the enumerated semantic errors, such as division by zero. It has its own model-error outcome.
Primary failurePlanning, provider, build, invocation or evaluation failed. It must retain its stage and diagnostic.
CancelledTerminal cancellation evidence, distinct from merely acknowledging a cancel request.
Cleanup failureSeparate evidence that can accompany any terminal result. It does not overwrite the primary cause or returned value.

A snapshot fixes what a job will execute. Editing the source, changing arguments, switching projects or reconnecting cannot rewrite an accepted job. Job and snapshot identities remain bound to their host, session and provider. Query does not execute again, and a terminal result is immutable.

Cancellation acknowledgement is an intermediate fact. A timeout or lost connection can leave work running, so the client retains its last receipt and avoids inventing failure, cancellation or safe-to-retry submission. The native host confirms worker exit and cleanup separately. A new page cannot borrow an old page's session or workspace grant.

The locally qualified Task 16.3 private Scheme job path captures the original source, ordered calls and arguments, complete selected boundary, runtime, provider and effective policy. A once-only claim gives the actual worker that retained selection. Replanning copies retained inputs into a new job, snapshot and plan identity; original jobs remain independent. Changing caller data or a later default cannot rewrite accepted work.

The first worker-plan mismatch stays a failure; a later matching message cannot clear it. Actual isolated Node worker tests cover this boundary separately from controlled in-memory traces. Surfaced UI controls and native/HTTP capability offers remain pending integrations.

The shared Rust Morphir Compatibility Kit owns the fixed cases, expected observations and compatibility verdicts. An explicit implementation adapter receives inputs, drives production behavior and returns observations. It receives neither expected results nor case IDs. The Rust checker reloads the exact corpus and recomputes qualification from the saved report.

This separates a requirement from the implementation being tested. A second verdict engine inside the Workbench would let both sides share the same mistaken assumptions.

Different evidence proves different things. Codec suites verify handling of values within their stated contracts; each actual value is still validated. Client suites verify scoped boundary behavior. Real worker exit, filesystem containment, authenticated connections and packaged acceptance use separate tests. Controlled completions do not establish real OS provenance or worker execution.

The Rust checker reloads the exact corpus and recomputes qualification from the saved report.

This separates a requirement from the implementation being tested. A second verdict engine inside the Workbench would let both sides share the same mistaken assumptions.

Different evidence proves different things. Codec suites verify handling of values within their stated contracts; each actual value is still validated. Client suites verify scoped boundary behavior. The 43-trace Owner suite drives actual Owner, Session and Workspace policy with controlled jobs Host and memory IO. Real worker exit, filesystem containment, authenticated connections and packaged acceptance use separate tests. Controlled completions do not establish real OS provenance or worker execution.

What is done and what is current

Delivered PR #117 was qualified at source 347df734 and squash merged as 4cb4c6de. Draft.11 and its narrow execution route remain unchanged.

Task 16.2 local qualification uses MoonBit core a0646a207c46b44198305cbd3ebf8adb5d2cd9a9, adapter e78ab4acdc455190598936f8a0de96951fa8f390 and parent source 3a9fd5db5d033402b1485af997e5870d52ab1a3b. These are the recorded local checks; they do not establish a public offer.

In controlled lost-reply traces, the reply is actually discarded. The trace view is separate trusted owner instrumentation, not a client-received reply, successful delivery, client knowledge or reconnect authority.

Checking policy for unsupported code

Task 16.2 delivers the Library-only Scheme behavior below. Task 16.3 delivers locally qualified private Scheme jobs and actual Node worker propagation. The full public integration workflow in the retained design diagram remains proposed. Strict stays the default; surfaced UI and existing native/HTTP offers remain strict. Their closed draft.1 mappings reject new fields.

The checking policy controls when unsupported semantic code is checked. Strict checks the whole model before execution; the locally qualified permissive Scheme path checks known unsupported code as it executes. Source integrity and the complete selected input/output types are validated under both policies. The timing choice does not weaken data or authority validation.

Model or execution situationStrict checking todayAs-executed checking, locally qualified
Supported public call in a supported libraryRun after validation and upfront support checking.Return the same typed result.
Unsupported declaration is unusedWhole-library preparation may reject.Prepare only the needed definitions after validating the selected public boundary.
Known unsupported expression is in an untaken branchPreparation may reject it.Do not execute it; use the taken branch normally.
The same unsupported expression is reachedExisting rejection.Fail at evaluation with execution.unsupported_reached.
Malformed source, ambiguous identities, private entry, wrong arguments or unsupported selected typesReject.Still reject. Unused code still counts toward source and resource limits.

Unused does not mean lazy. An eager argument or binding executes even when nobody uses its result. An uncalled lambda and an untaken conditional branch are different. The complete selected input/output type closure remains mandatory, including alternatives absent from the particular value.

The new reached-unsupported failure is a primary failed / evaluate outcome. It is neither an SDK ModelError nor a successful typed Result.Err. Parser errors, exhausted budgets, missing authorized bindings and provider failures retain their own diagnostics. This interpreter path does not prune source, expand host authority or qualify generated JavaScript, Wasm or native execution.

Interpreter fuel, frame and depth budgets remain enforced, but opaque SDK internals can allocate memory or consume CPU before another interpreter check. Fuel is not a hard process CPU or allocation quota; follow-up morphir-be5t tracks that gap.

Task 3 integrates native MEP PR #127 from main at 3b7ccd0. That adapter compiles the existing MoonBit Boolean library profile into a rich model with source provenance. It negotiates compilation separately from generation and does not enable Workbench permissive jobs, expand portable source syntax or complete Tasks 4–6. Upstream setup PR #129 at 83283be is also integrated. Its Unix installation and Linux ARM64 checks add no packaged desktop policy claim. Native process compilation and the generated consumer pass on the integrated tree; the independent Scheme job corpus still qualifies in all six lanes. The subsequent PR #130 at cac8f85 is integrated too. It adds the preferred dated cumulative MoonBit Bool/String/Int32 profile and affects Scheme SDK/type boundaries. A new regression compiles that profile and executes String/Int32 jobs through actual workers under both policies. Task 4 now explicitly preserves source-profile selections/drafts separately from checking policy and tests their composition; the six-task sequence and completion count remain unchanged. Native MEP still has its separately negotiated Boolean profile.

Standalone capability controls

Task 4 is delivered in PR #133, merged as ef28cc3 with a tree identical to qualified source 823f426. All 36 checks passed with 2 intentional skips and no actionable review findings. Select a public function and choose Typed invocation. Capability checks defaults to Whole model before running. Choosing As code executes lets supported paths run while unsupported operations remain unused. Reaching one returns a failed result with its diagnostic. Both policies validate the complete selected input/output boundary, including signed Int32 bounds.

The browser retains the compiled or imported IR even when generation fails. A fresh worker captures the model, arguments and policy, builds its immutable plan and validates the returned terminal. Changing inputs or policy while it runs leaves the captured result intact and marks it stale. Cancellation stops that worker and late replies are discarded. Source profiles and JSON/Ion drafts stay separate from checking policy. Native and HTTP mappings remain strict until Tasks 5 and 6 qualify them.

Six implementation phases

4 of 6 merged, 66.7%. Done: 4. Remaining: 2. Next are native Proton and authenticated HTTP policy mappings.

PhaseWhat it will deliverStatus
1. Selected-entry planA private bounded Scheme plan evaluates a supported public Int42 call beside valid, unused unsupported code. Strict remains unchanged.Delivered, Task 16.1
2. Reached-only semanticsUntaken branches succeed; reached known unsupported operations fail predictably. Qualify the complete local policy corpus before exposing capability.Delivered, Task 16.2

4. Standalone UIOffer an explicit policy choice only for a qualified local runtime, with compatible drafts and existing result/diagnostic controls.Delivered, Task 16.4; PR #133

6. Authenticated HTTPNegotiate and prove policy through an actual job-enabled gateway/provider. Existing Rust connected-v1 behavior remains unchanged.Pending, after 3 and 4

Approved design · Detailed implementation plan · Delivered Owner architecture and evidence limits

Evidence and scope

The design baseline is MoonBit e02cf5f and parent Morphir a14e7c62. Recent source-node inventory changes affect metadata ownership bookkeeping; they do not create public-call or native-execution authority. The permissive plan must derive public boundaries from authoritative IR.

Mac packaged acceptance does not establish Linux or Windows GUI conformance. Controlled Owner tests do not prove real worker exit or filesystem races. design:
Skip to specification
Morphir / MoonBit

A2 + F4 integration
Specification revision 0.12
17 October 2026

01 / Outcome and status02 / Current contract evidence03 / Component ownership04 / Guest runtime choice05 / Ion and checked JSON06 / MEP gap analysis07 / MEP call flows08 / Claims and sessions09 / Packaging and installation10 / Implementation slices11 / Acceptance matrix12 / Sources and records
Pluggable library pipeline / extension delivery

Deliver the MoonBit pipeline to an upstream Morphir host.

Package the existing frontend and generator behind a thin extension adapter, retain native Ion models, and prove installation and use through an independently pinned host.

P1/P2 + shared P3 runtime landedLanguage: moonbitNumeric work independentIon preferred; JSON supported

Owned by A2 morphir-ukvn.1.3 and F4 morphir-ukvn.1.10.5. Compatibility study morphir-ukvn.1.3.1. P1 native bundling and P2 installed legacy-backend qualification have landed. P3a landed in canonical PR #1051. P3b SDK/host runtime landed in Rust PR #302, bead morphir-opua.1.3.1.2. Installed MoonBit rich round trips, portable guest qualification and F4 completion remain outstanding.

01 / outcome

Move from an in-process implementation to an installable provider

The local engine and CLI already compile Boolean MoonBit libraries, retain source and naming metadata, evaluate them, and generate callable libraries. F4 makes that functionality available through the ecosystem extension lifecycle. It uses the same pure components; it does not create a second compiler.

First useful installed flow

  1. Build and bundle a pinned MoonBit guest.
  2. Publish to a controlled test extension index.
  3. Install into an isolated upstream MORPHIR_HOME.
  4. Negotiate an existing Boolean library profile.
  5. Compile source into a rich MorphirModel, then generate a library.
  6. Compile and invoke a consumer; retain origins and exact evidence.

Separate completion states

The native bundler landed in Morphir #1050 at d74a506a; the MoonBit native backend landed in MoonBit #107 at 1f91ec2. Numeric implementation belongs to issue #98. Neither completes F4.

A2 supplies a reusable language-neutral packaging contract. F4 supplies the MoonBit guest and installed acceptance. B2/B3 retain the WIT/component roadmap. A native proof does not complete those component milestones.

Remaining integration gap. Language-neutral native bundling and an installed MoonBit legacy backend are implemented. The canonical model contract has landed. SDK and shared host transport/admission landed in PR #302; the MoonBit rich adapter and installed qualification remain to be implemented. An ordinary MoonBit WASM build and an extra JSON response member do not close those gaps.

02 / pinned evidence

Distinguish existing contracts from proposed additions

BoundaryObserved nowRequired integration
Upstream hostprocess channels use Content-Length-framed JSON-RPC. wasm uses Extism and requires its guest ABI.Choose and qualify the actual guest adapter. Keep runtime identity independent from artifact acquisition.
WASM ABIThe host calls morphir_extension_info and handle. The Rust SDK generates Extism exports.A MoonBit WASM adapter needs its own proven Extism imports, exports, memory and session behavior. WASI or Wasm-GC output is not that proof.
Native bundlingmorphir extension bundle accepts explicit executable, identity, version and native platform inputs; it probes exact bytes and stages an atomic three-file bundle without Cargo assumptions.P1 landed in #1050. Runtime/platform expansion and complete A2/F4 acceptance remain separately scoped.
VersionsFrozen legacy MEP 0.1; model-operation draft 0.2.0-draft.1; envelope 0.1.0-draft.1; claims 0.1.0-draft.2; bundle 2.0.0-draft.2.New model methods require the exact full-SemVer draft and bilateral tuple agreement. Contract declarations do not establish runtime support.
Compile resultThe compiled SDK probe drops an unrecognized top-level unit member during typed round trip.Define and negotiate explicit model operations in the canonical model, SDK, host and guest. Do not rely on unknown-field survival.
OptionsCompile vendor profile options and opaque generation option values survive SDK serialization.This permits explicit profile selection, but does not prove host propagation or authorize an undocumented metadata tunnel.
Request IDsThe SDK accepts unsigned numeric IDs; it rejects a string ID even though the canonical model includes string IDs.Test against the pinned SDK subset and separately resolve the model/implementation discrepancy before claiming general ID support.

Rust source snapshot 6a481ec17cf75d889ad363b008ece2ba0ea6e05f; ecosystem specification snapshot 5975da737b210c958ef57114a78dc6830bf67559; MoonBit work snapshot 9cf80a00ec694460c61e4bf16996cf67ee90aac5. The SDK probe uses Rust 1.98.1 and compiles actual source from the pinned archive. It does not activate a host.

Probe artifacts: SDK observations, MoonBit data-boundary observations, and primary evidence in Ion text. Binary Ion is the primary stored receipt. Exact code, lock and result digests are in that receipt.

03 / composition

Keep transport and distribution outside the pure pipeline

ComponentOwnsContract
Build driverPinned compiler/core, dependency trees and selected target; produces immutable guest bytes.Build identity is separate from extension capabilities. No registry download is hidden inside compilation.
A2 packagerArtifact inventory, hashes, actual guest describe probe, descriptor checks and atomic local staging.Receives explicit build/version inputs. Does not fabricate claims or require a Rust source layout.
HostResolve/install/activate, identity and capability checks, operation admission, process lifetime, workspace writes.Only invoke after negotiation. Local source-provider authentication and naming authority remain explicit.
Guest transportBounded frames, JSON-RPC envelope, lifecycle state, dispatch, diagnostic mapping and payload codecs.No logs on protocol stdout. The transport owns I/O and passes values into pure APIs.
Pure frontend and generatorParse, resolve, check, lower, metadata production and IR-to-artifact generation.Reuse existing library APIs and limits. No filesystem, host resolution or implicit executable lookup.
Model payload codecValidate negotiated profile, identity, size, digest and Ion envelope; check JSON loss.Unknown node metadata survives. Metadata cannot register behavior or grant host privileges.
04 / runtime

Propose a native process first, retain a portable guest path

Native backend adapter landed

The MoonBit native MEP process entry point is implemented for the legacy backend flow. Its build/bundle tasks use explicit platform artifacts and preserve identity/capability checks. Rich frontend/model methods follow shared SDK/host adoption; each platform still requires its own qualification.

A process keeps the ambient OS rights of its user. Clearing its environment is not a sandbox. Pure compiler boundaries remain valuable, but must not be advertised as process isolation. Network access, workspace reads and provider authority are not granted by annotations.

Portable core WASM, after an ABI proof

Implement or select a MoonBit Extism adapter only after a real host can call both required exports, exchange UTF-8 bytes, preserve session state and enforce budgets. Probe memory/import compatibility, error propagation and repeated calls. Keep that adapter replaceable; a native first delivery does not remove it from the roadmap.

Component-model target remains separate

B2 morphir-ukvn.2.2 defines MEP as WIT; B3 morphir-ukvn.2.3 proves component extensions. Both are open. The current host describes Extism, not a WIT/component runtime. Preserve those milestones and their acceptance; do not relabel an Extism or process artifact as a component.

The runtime selector remains process or wasm where those are the upstream contract values. Language remains moonbit; the generated target remains moonbit. Library/profile capabilities are separately negotiated. Production guest and package entry-point names will be fixed in the implementation plan.

05 / data preservation

Negotiate native models explicitly

Use model for the logical value and envelope for its representation

TermMeaning in this design

Accepted terminology for the proposed public contract is MorphirModel, morphir.frontend.compileModel and morphir.backend.generateModel. Compile consumes a compilation unit and returns a model; generation consumes a model and returns artifacts. The model also remains useful for transformations, validation and evaluation.

Current implementation mapping. The existing MoonBit engine type is data.IRUnit. The public contract uses MorphirModel as the domain name; IR describes its underlying semantic representation. Its current Ion profile uses contract: "ir-unit" and unit_id. Those existing API and stored-format names remain accurate in source references and historical probe evidence. This design adopts the public model vocabulary; any implementation rename needs a separate source-compatibility and stored-format migration decision. New method and wire-field spellings require upstream agreement.

JSON-RPC may remain the control protocol while a negotiated payload carries binary Ion. The logical pipeline value is a MorphirModel with distribution, node metadata, ordered annotations and provenance. Preserve exact integers, Decimal scale, unknown neighbors and original naming facts.

Legacy operations retain their current JSON IR fields.

    envelopeVersion: "0.1.0-draft.1",

The canonical contract slice defines these fields and wire mappings. They are draft declarations; SDK/host implementation and executable conformance follow separately.

  1. Host and guest both advertise and understand the same model transport contract. Required/critical members must fail on older readers rather than be ignored.
  2. The admitted profile, codec, envelope revision and IR version form one supported tuple, frozen for the operation. No retry silently substitutes JSON after an Ion refusal.
  3. Validate frame size before allocation, base64 expansion and decoded byte length before parsing, then SHA-256, envelope identity and tree limits.
  4. Decode to the current engine representation and call the existing pure APIs. Return artifacts and structured diagnostics; the host decides when to write them.
  5. For legacy JSON, use the checked codec. A rich source-produced model that cannot be exported fails with the existing data.lossy_conversion diagnostic. Do not strip metadata to make a legacy host appear compatible.

Backward compatibility. Existing JSON IR backend requests remain supported where they are lossless. A legacy host may exercise that backend path, but it cannot be described as supporting rich MoonBit frontend round trips. An opaque generation option surviving serialization is not a negotiated transport.

Model variants and checked states evolve independently

A pipeline enriches a Morphir model through explicit transitions. Reuse the existing Distribution variants for library, specification and application content. Represent established guarantees through checked states or views, with runtime evidence at configurable component and MEP boundaries. A single parsed/resolved/typed/validated/optimized enum would conflate independent properties and imply one fixed pipeline order.

RepresentationIon, JSON and document-tree choices belong to model envelopes. They do not define semantic model states.

Each component declares what it requires, establishes, preserves and invalidates. Evidence identifies the model revision, dependency context, scope and producer. A structural rewrite may invalidate type or analysis evidence, even when it retains source metadata. Preservation must follow an explicit component contract; it cannot be assumed from a stage label such as optimized.

Within an implementation, checked constructors or views can enforce component prerequisites. Across MEP, received state labels and evidence are claims until the host admits them under its checking and trust policy. An unknown required guarantee prevents invocation; an opaque optional enrichment can remain preserved. Language-level extensibility does not replace protocol negotiation or grant authority. Select a tuple before invoking a component

  1. Describe declares supported model operations and exact supported tuples. The language is moonbit; a Boolean-library profile describes capabilities separately.
  2. Initialize carries optional host modelTransport offers; negotiated capabilities return optional guest modelTransport support restricted to the offered tuples. Each includes complete tuples, limits and interpreted guarantee IDs. Freeze the admissible set for the session. Missing offers mean legacy-only; support for a guarantee ID does not establish it.
  3. Each model operation selects one tuple from that set. Validate the method, profile, codec, envelope revision, semantic IR version and limits together before invoking pure compiler APIs.
  4. The host retains the resulting model and its identity. It forwards the complete payload to the next admitted consumer. If that consumer has no compatible tuple, refuse that handoff without dropping metadata.

New-draft admission rules. A selected modelTransport may narrow the extension's static claims: tuples and interpreted guarantee IDs are subsets of both claims and host offers, and selected limits cannot exceed either. This is a specific exception for the new exact MEP draft; legacy capability equality remains unchanged. The current SDK claim/session checker still compares arrays and scalar values exactly and requires follow-up alignment.

The selected operation tuple authorizes compileModel or generateModel. Frontend language/source-count and backend target capabilities still apply. Legacy compile/generate booleans authorize their legacy methods; they do not force a rich-only provider to advertise unsupported legacy operations.

The payload identifies its envelope contract revision, semantic IR version, logical model ID, codec, decoded byte length, digest and encoded content. For JSON-RPC, binary Ion bytes use base64; future WIT uses a byte sequence. The digest binds the exact payload bytes after base64 decoding and before profile parsing, not the base64 spelling or semantic equivalence between codecs. Model identity and logical revision remain separate. Verify consistency with the decoded envelope and negotiated tuple. Compression, chunking and out-of-band file references are not prerequisites for this first flow.

Aggregate budgets. maxEncodedBytes and maxDecodedBytes bound the sum of all model, dependency and evidence payloads in one request or response, as well as each payload. Encoded bytes count base64 content; decoded bytes count the resulting bytes. maxDepth applies to each decoded document with its root at depth one; maxNodes bounds total decoded value nodes. Many small evidence entries cannot bypass the operation's budget. Independent frame/parser bounds still apply before allocation.

Transport preservation and transformation semantics differ. A forwarding host must retain unknown facts exactly. A transform must declare what it changes, retain unrelated metadata, and record lineage or invalidate facts whose owners it replaces. Source number precision and original/target naming can travel as metadata without granting provider authority or changing the consumer's numeric semantics.

Critical members must identify the feature actually required

The claim reader rejects an unknown exact critical path. Marking only capabilities or capabilities.frontend as critical does not make unknown children understood. Register the precise model-contract requirement and its validation semantics. Older readers must reject a guest that requires it; an optional model feature may remain unavailable while legacy operations still work.

Claim/session agreement permits a session to omit unselected capabilities. Keep that behavior. Model admission must independently require explicit selected support. A requires.host version comparator is useful for known implementation requirements, but cannot substitute for negotiating the feature.

Preserve provenance identity so original-name hints still apply.Actual frontend output retains public names, references and origins through the carrier. Linked target names work with injected authenticated capabilities and refuse with metadata.provider_unavailable without them. Wire metadata grants no authority.
generateModelDecode an explicit semantic view for generator.Input, retaining the rich model separately. Reuse existing artifact and diagnostic serialization.Fixed rich fixture retains annotations, large integers, decimal scale and unknown facts byte-for-byte. Equivalent plain IR produces equivalent generated code in a real native SDK session.
compileModel and orchestrationWrap the existing frontend result with explicit identity, revision and enrichments. Then enable deliberate rich CLI routing and installed qualification through the existing MCK.Installed compile → retain → generate → consumer flow, explicit checked JSON compatibility and scoped refusal cases.
The engine checkpoint and MEP model are different contracts

The stored engine envelope is morphir_pipeline::{profile, contract: "ir-unit", unit_id, ir, metadata, provenance}. The MEP payload is morphir_model::{ir, enrichments, provenance}; its identity and revision live in the outer transport envelope. Engine metadata uses {node_id, data}, while MEP enrichments use {owner, data}. A namespace owner cannot be cast to a node identity.

The adapter must preserve unknown optional content and original bytes. It cannot round-trip the rich payload through the engine checkpoint codec or a generic Ion-to-JSON conversion. MEP depth starts at one, excludes annotations and field names from node counts, and aggregates model/evidence budgets. The engine's post-decode traversal uses different conventions. Required remote guarantees remain refused under the current default evidence policy. Arbitrary retained enrichments are not automatically generator node metadata or symbols.10n content.

P4 / installed qualification

Prove local index, install, compile and generation

Use independently pinned host bytes and fresh installation state. Exercise seed/library profiles, naming, pure components, generated consumers, metadata replay and failure behavior. Record each repository's actual commit range and each supported OS/target/mode separately.

Portable route / B2 and B3 remain open

Qualify the agreed WASM or component adapter

Run a real Extism ABI spike before choosing that adapter. Follow B2/B3 for WIT/component integration. Native-process qualification does not waive an agreed portable-guest acceptance requirement. Close F4 only against the agreed A2 transport and full installed evidence.

# Scheme language reference as package-level docs: implementation plan

Plan: .dev/beads-plans/morphir-ukvn.5.45.4-plan.html (HTML, per AGENTS.md). Spec: the design of morphir-ukvn.5.45.4.
design:
Scheme language reference as package-level docs: implementation plan

Bead morphir-ukvn.5.45.4 · plan drafted 2026-10-16 · spec .dev/beads-specs/morphir-ukvn.5.45.4.html

For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task by task. Each step is one action.
  • Overview
  • Global constraints
  • Review focus
  • File structure
  • Task 1: site package pages
  • Task 2: example extractor
  • Task 3: chapters and generated tests
  • Task 4: core language chapter
  • Task 5: writing models chapter
  • Task 6: running Morphir IR chapter
  • Task 7: scripts and spec chapters
  • Task 8: site, publish and wrap-up

Overview

Goal: a detailed Morphir Scheme language reference, one README.mbt.md chapter per package, shown on mooncakes and on the project site, with every ```scheme example run by moon test.

Architecture: the site learns README.mbt.md and sub-package pages. A native tool in the unpublished finos/morphir-typing-tools module turns each chapter's Scheme examples into a generated docs_examples_test.mbt; a short hand-written run_example per package decides how an example runs. Today's pkgs/morphir-scheme/README.md is split into the five chapters, which then grow into a full reference.

Tech stack: MoonBit 0.10.15, moonbitlang/x 0.5.5 (fs, sys), moonbitlang/async 0.22.1 for scripts, the site's Bun and TypeScript build, moonrockz/expect 0.6.1 for new hand-written tests.

Spec: .dev/beads-specs/morphir-ukvn.5.45.4.html. Read it with this plan.

Branch: a new branch from origin/main in its own worktree (for example DamianReeves/scheme-language-docs); never the merged metadata branch.

Global constraints

  • No Scheme behaviour changes. An example that exposes a bug gets a bead; the example is changed to today's behaviour or marked notest with the bead id.
  • Every paragraph of today's pkgs/morphir-scheme/README.md lands in a chapter; Task 3 records the mapping.
  • Generated files start with // GENERATED by `mise run scheme-docs:generate` from <chapter>. Do not edit.
  • Generated tests run on native, js, wasm and wasm-gc.
  • Commits use Conventional Commits in plain English, with no AI attribution and no Co-Authored-By line.
  • On this machine: run ~/.moon/bin/moon.exe; for Bun use C:\Users\damre\AppData\Local\mise\installs\bun\1.4.2\bin\bun.exe; prepend C:\Users\damre\AppData\Local\mise\installs\node\24.21.0 to PATH for js tests. The mise shims fail on Windows ARM64.
  • Module test runs use -p per package (a module directory still tests the whole workspace). moon fmt and moon info touch every package: restore unrelated files before committing.
  • Chapters follow the repository's writing rules: plain English, one idea per sentence, tables for parallel facts.

Review focus

  1. Windows line endings. A chapter checked out with CRLF must give the same examples and the same generated file as LF. Pinned in Task 2 (extractor) and Task 2's check mode (compare without \r).
  2. Indented fences. A ```scheme fence indented inside a list item would silently escape testing. The extractor refuses an indented ```scheme fence with its line. Pinned in Task 2.
  3. Quotes and backslashes in expectations. A string result such as "a\"b" must survive into the generated MoonBit literal. Pinned in Task 2.
  4. Other packages' sub-READMEs. Turning every listed package's sub-package README into a page also publishes pkgs/morphir-engine/{data,elm,ids,moonbit,execution/jobs}/README.md and pkgs/morphir-sdk/conformance/README.md; broken links or titles there must not break the build. Pinned in Task 1, Step 6 (full site build).
  5. Both README kinds in one directory. Two sources for one route must fail with a clear message, not a generic duplicate-route error. Pinned in Task 1.

    ///|
pub(all) suberror DocError {
  DocError(String)
}

///|
pub(all) enum Expect {
  Value(String)
  Fails(String)
  Runs
} derive(Eq, Debug)

///|
pub(all) struct Example {
  files : Array[(String, String)]
  expect : Expect
  line : Int
} derive(Eq, Debug)

///|
pub(all) struct Chapter {
  examples : Array[Example]
  skipped : Int
  procedures : Array[String]
}

///|
fn strip_cr(line : String) -> String {
  if line.has_suffix("\r") {
    line[:line.length() - 1].to_owned()
  } else {
    line
  }
}

///|
/// The expectation of a block: its last non-empty line.
fn expectation(body : Array[String]) -> Expect {
  let mut i = body.length() - 1
  while i >= 0 && body[i] == "" {
    i -= 1
  }
  if i < 0 {
    return Runs
  }
  let last = body[i]
  if last.has_prefix(";; => ") {
    Value(last[6:].to_owned())
  } else if last.has_prefix(";; error: ") {
    Fails(last[10:].to_owned())
  } else {
    Runs
  }
}

///|
/// The line without its leading spaces.
fn without_indent(line : String) -> String {
  let mut i = 0
  while i < line.length() && line.code_unit_at(i).to_int() == 32 {
    i += 1
  }
  line[i:].to_owned()
}

///|
/// Whether the next ```scheme block at or after line index `from` starts with `;; file:`.
fn next_scheme_block_is_file(lines : Array[String], from : Int) -> Bool {
  for j in from..<lines.length() {
    if lines[j] == "```scheme" {
      return j + 1 < lines.length() && lines[j + 1].has_prefix(";; file: ")
    }
  }
  false
}

///|
fn first_code(line : String) -> String? {
  guard line.find("`") is Some(start) else { return None }
  let rest = line[start + 1:].to_owned()
  guard rest.find("`") is Some(end) else { return None }
  Some(rest[:end].to_owned())
}

///|
pub fn parse_chapter(text : String) -> Chapter raise DocError {
  let lines : Array[String] = text.split("\n").map(l => strip_cr(l.to_owned())).collect()
  let examples : Array[Example] = []
  let procedures : Array[String] = []
  let mut skipped = 0
  let mut in_procedures = false
  // A project of `;; file:` blocks that is still open: its files, first line, and a block with an expectation.
  let project : Array[(String, String)] = []
  let mut project_line = 0
  fn close_project(expect : Expect) -> Unit {
    if !project.is_empty() {
      examples.push({ files: project.copy(), expect, line: project_line })
      project.clear()
    }
  }
  let mut i = 0
  while i < lines.length() {
    let line = lines[i]
    if line.has_prefix("## ") {
      in_procedures = line == "## Built-in procedures"
    } else if in_procedures && line.has_prefix("| `") {
      if first_code(line) is Some(name) {
        procedures.push(name)
      }
    }
    if !line.has_prefix("```") && without_indent(line).has_prefix("```scheme") {
      raise DocError("line \{i + 1}: indented scheme block")
    }
    if line.has_prefix("```") {
      let open_line = i + 1
      let info = line[3:].to_owned().split(" ").filter(w => w != "").map(w => w.to_owned()).collect()
      let body : Array[String] = []
      i += 1
      while i < lines.length() && !lines[i].has_prefix("```") {
        body.push(lines[i])
        i += 1
      }
      if i == lines.length() {
        raise DocError("line \{open_line}: unclosed code block")
      }
      match info {
        ["scheme"] => {
          let expect = expectation(body)
          let source = body.join("\n")
          if body.length() > 0 && body[0].has_prefix(";; file: ") {
            if project.is_empty() {
              project_line = open_line
            }
            project.push((body[0][9:].to_owned(), source))
            if !(expect is Runs) {
              if next_scheme_block_is_file(lines, i + 1) {
                raise DocError(
                  "line \{project_line}: only the last file: block of a project may state an expectation",
                )
              }
              close_project(expect)
            }
          } else {
            close_project(Runs)
            examples.push({ files: [("", source)], expect, line: open_line })
          }
        }
        ["scheme", "notest"] => skipped += 1
        _ => ()
      }
    }
    i += 1
  }
  close_project(Runs)
  { examples, skipped, procedures }
}

    ///|
fn literal(text : String) -> String {
  "\"" +
  text
  .replace_all(old="\\", new="\\\\")
  .replace_all(old="\"", new="\\\"")
  .replace_all(old="\n", new="\\n") +
  "\""
}

///|
fn expect_source(expect : Expect) -> String {
  match expect {
    Value(v) => "Value(\{literal(v)})"
    Fails(m) => "Fails(\{literal(m)})"
    Runs => "Runs"
  }
}

///|
pub fn render_examples(chapter_name : String, chapter : Chapter) -> String {
  let out = StringBuilder()
  out.write_string(
    "// GENERATED by `mise run scheme-docs:generate` from \{chapter_name}. Do not edit.\n",
  )
  out.write_string(
    "// \{chapter.examples.length()} checked examples; \{chapter.skipped} notest blocks.\n",
  )
  out.write_string(harness)
  out.write_string("\n")
  for n, example in chapter.examples {
    out.write_string(
      "\n///|\ntest \"\{chapter_name} example \{n + 1} (line \{example.line})\" {\n  check_example(\n    [\n",
    )
    for file in example.files {
      out.write_string("      (\n        \{literal(file.0)},\n")
      for source_line in file.1.split("\n") {
        out.write_string("      #|\{source_line}\n")
      }
      out.write_string("      ),\n")
    }
    out.write_string(
      "    ],\n    \{expect_source(example.expect)},\n    line=\{example.line},\n  )\n}\n",
    )
  }
  out.to_string()
}

///|
pub fn render_procedures(chapter_name : String, chapter : Chapter) -> String? {
  if chapter.procedures.is_empty() {
    return None
  }
  let names = chapter.procedures.map(literal).join(", ")
  Some(
    "// GENERATED by `mise run scheme-docs:generate` from \{chapter_name}. Do not edit.\n\n///|\nlet documented_procedures : Array[String] = [\{names}]\n",
  )
}

///|
pub fn difference(expected : String, actual : String) -> String? {
  let a = expected.replace_all(old="\r", new="").split("\n").map(l => l.to_owned()).collect()
  let b = actual.replace_all(old="\r", new="").split("\n").map(l => l.to_owned()).collect()
  for i in 0..<a.length() {
    if i >= b.length() {
      return Some("line \{i + 1}: expected `\{a[i]}`, found end of file")
    }
    if a[i] != b[i] {
      return Some("line \{i + 1}: expected `\{a[i]}`, found `\{b[i]}`")
    }
  }
  if b.length() > a.length() {
    Some("line \{a.length() + 1}: expected end of file, found `\{b[a.length()]}`")
  } else {
    None
  }
}

let chapters : Array[String] = [
  "pkgs/morphir-scheme/README.mbt.md", "pkgs/morphir-scheme/frontend/README.mbt.md",
  "pkgs/morphir-scheme/backend/README.mbt.md", "pkgs/morphir-scheme/pipeline/README.mbt.md",

///|
/// Each chapter's generated files: (path, text).
fn outputs() -> Array[(String, String)] raise {
  let result = []
  for path in chapters {
    let dir = path[:path.length() - "/README.mbt.md".length()].to_owned()
    let chapter = parse_chapter(@fs.read_file_to_string(path))
    result.push((dir + "/docs_examples_test.mbt", render_examples(path, chapter)))
    if render_procedures(path, chapter) is Some(text) {
      result.push((dir + "/docs_procedures_generated_wbtest.mbt", text))
    }
  }
  result
}

///|
fn main {
  let args = @env.args()
  let rest = args[1:].to_owned()
  try {
    match rest {
      ["generate"] =>
        for output in outputs() {
          @fs.write_string_to_file(output.0, output.1)
          println("wrote \{output.0}")
        }
      ["check"] => {
        let problems = []
        for output in outputs() {
          let current = @fs.read_file_to_string(output.0) catch { _ => "" }
          if difference(output.1, current) is Some(d) {
            problems.push("\{output.0}: \{d}")
          }
        }
        if problems.is_empty() {
          println("scheme docs examples are current")
        } else {
          for p in problems {
            println(p)
          }
          println("schemedocs: run `mise run scheme-docs:generate`")
          @sys.exit(1)
        }
      }
      _ => {
        println("usage: schemedocs generate | check")
        @sys.exit(2)
      }
    }
  } catch {
    DocError(message) => {
      println("schemedocs: \{message}")
      @sys.exit(1)
    }
    e => {
      println("schemedocs: \{e}")
      @sys.exit(1)
    }
  }
}

///|
/// Compile each file in file mode; run the last one's `main` when it has trailing expressions.
fn run_example(files : Array[(String, String)]) -> String raise {
  let mut last = ""
  for file in files {
    let module_name = module_of(file.0)
    let ir = @frontend.compile_file(file.1, module_name~)
    last = if has_main(ir) {
      @scheme.value_to_string(
        @backend.run_file(ir, @ir.FQName::parse("user:" + module_name + "#main"), []),
      )
    } else {
      ""
    }
  }
  last
}

///|
fn module_of(path : String) -> String {
  if path == "" {
    return "main"
  }
  let p = if path.has_prefix("src/") { path[4:].to_owned() } else { path }
  match p.rev_find(".") {
    Some(i) => p[:i].to_owned()
    None => p
  }
}

///|
fn has_main(ir : @ir.IRFile) -> Bool {
  guard ir.distribution is Library(_, _, definition) else { return false }
  definition.modules.values().any(m => m.value.values.contains(@ir.Name::parse("main")))
}

title: F4 P3c: expose rich model generation through native MEP
description: Add exact opt-in MEP0.2.0-draft.1 generateModel to the native MoonBit adapter around the existing pure generator. Keep legacy MEP0.1 unchanged. Implement exact bilateral tuple selection and frozen session limits, canonical base64 and byte SHA-256 validation, aggregate model/evidence budgets, critical-member refusal and original-byte retention. Decode the morphir_model Ion wrapper explicitly; engine morphir_pipeline IRUnit checkpoints are a different contract, and namespace owner cannot be cast to node_id. Refuse required remote guarantees under current default policy. Reuse upgraded moonrockz/ion0.5.0 reader protection at128 nested containers and its stack-safe walkers. Before advertising Ion, establish remaining negotiated pre-materialization node, symbol-table and aggregate byte/evidence limits; event readers still decode full containers, so post-decode tree budgets remain insufficient. Reconcile negotiated depth with the fixed reader ceiling and prefer reusable Ion-package support. Avoid generator-to-engine/host module cycles; extract shared byte SHA-256 into a lower layer if necessary. Preserve unknown enrichments separately and do not claim they reach symbols.10n without explicit mapping. Do not add a second MCK runner. Follow rich generation with separate compileModel and CLI-orchestration slices. Baseline root is main00e4d36, including the Ion0.5.0 upgrade in PR116. SDK adoption and Ion-upgrade prerequisites have landed; rich operations remain unimplemented.

Specification revision 0.15
