title: Unified extension SDK for guest and host sides across runtimes (Rust, TypeScript, Python)
description: Follow-up from the single-file synthesis work (finos/morphir#915, #917). Today the portable workspace discovery rules (selection confinement, duplicate rejection, name-required, empty language) live only in Rust (morphir-workspace). The morphir-elm MEP extension (TypeScript, vnext) gets a minimal hand port of the ad-hoc subset so it can synthesize, which duplicates those rules. Build one SDK covering both the guest side (extension authors) and the host side (protocol types, discovery validation, compile envelope) for several runtimes, early targets Rust, TypeScript and Python, so providers stop re-porting protocol rules. Retire the TS hand port once the TS SDK exists.
design:
# Cross-language extension SDK Local working notes. Decided checkpoints are published at https://github.com/finos/morphir/discussions/949. This file is gitignored. Code blocks marked "sketch" show the shape of an idea. They are not a final API. ## Checkpoint 1. Scope The design is one extension SDK for the guest side and the host side, with early targets Rust, TypeScript, and Python. The Rust CLI is the first consumer. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph SDK["Extension SDK (morphir-opua)"] direction TB H["Host side
Rust first, then TypeScript, Python"] G["Guest side
Rust, TypeScript, Python"] end CLI["morphir CLI
(first consumer)"] --> H H <-->|MEP| G G --- Elm["Elm guest"] G --- Gleam["Gleam guest"] ``` The session-host extraction and the public compile entry points in finos/morphir#897 stay outside this thread, except where the SDK gives those callers a type they can use. The first rule already accepted for this SDK is the Elm explicit package-name normal form, in kb `morphir-extensions` decision 0005. `My.Package`, `My/Package`, and `my/package` all report `my/package`. The Rust copy is `normalize_package_name` on the Elm `SourceIdentity` in `morphir-elm-binding`. The shared checks around it live in `morphir-workspace` (`discover_with_identity`). The CLI already calls that crate. Decision 0005 also records a TypeScript copy in finos/morphir-elm and a Scala copy in morphir-scala-elm. The decision says the rule and its cases move into the SDK, and the providers drop their own copies. Scala is not an early target of `morphir-opua`. The case table still has to be something Scala can adopt. The rule today, from `morphir-elm-binding/src/workspace/mod.rs`: ```rust fn normalize_package_name(&self, name: &str) -> std::result::Result { let pieces: Vec<&str> = name .split(['/', '.']) .map(str::trim) .filter(|piece| !piece.is_empty()) // ... ``` The case table that every copy must pass: | Input | Reported name | | --- | --- | | `My.Package` | `my/package` | | `My/Package` | `my/package` | | `my/package` | `my/package` | ```mermaid flowchart LR Rule["Case table
(decision 0005)"] Rule --> Rust["Rust
morphir-elm-binding"] Rule --> TS["TypeScript
finos/morphir-elm"] Rule -.->|later| Scala["Scala
morphir-scala-elm"] ``` The issue also names protocol types, discovery validation, and the compile envelope, on both the guest side and the host side. Those are separate pieces. The next checkpoint names which piece is designed first. ## Checkpoint 2. First piece The first piece is the host API. The Rust CLI calls it in the first slice. The TypeScript and Python host ports are part of the same design and are built later. Today the CLI has two handshake paths. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph CLI["crates/morphir (today)"] E["extensions.rs
compile, generate, discovery"] P["commands/extension/probe.rs
install probe"] end E -->|"initialize
peer: morphir-cli
versions: MEP_VERSION"| Guest1["guest process"] P -->|"describe, then session fallback
peer: host_peer()
versions: SUPPORTED_MEP_VERSIONS"| Guest2["guest process"] P --> CS["check_statement
(morphir-extension-sdk)"] ``` `crates/morphir/src/extensions.rs` builds the provider registry and invokes compile, generate, and workspace discovery. It can hold a frontend or backend session open. `probe_process` starts a configured process, initializes it, and reads the negotiated capabilities. That path introduces the host as peer name `morphir-cli` and advertises one protocol version, `MEP_VERSION`: ```rust // crates/morphir/src/extensions.rs fn host_initialize_params() -> InitializeParams { InitializeParams { protocol_versions: vec![MEP_VERSION.into()], host: PeerInfo { name: "morphir-cli".into(), version: env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION").into(), }, } } ``` `crates/morphir/src/commands/extension/probe.rs` probes an artifact during install. It calls `describe`, falls back to a session, and checks the answer with `check_statement` in `morphir-extension-sdk`. That path uses `host_peer()` and advertises `SUPPORTED_MEP_VERSIONS`: ```rust // crates/morphir/src/commands/extension/probe.rs let description = transport .describe(InitializeParams { protocol_versions: SUPPORTED_MEP_VERSIONS .iter() .map(|version| (*version).into()) .collect(), host: super::host_peer(), }) .await?; ``` The two paths send different peer names and different version lists to the same guest. The host API gives both paths one handshake. The next checkpoint decides how much of this the CLI still writes. ## Checkpoint 3. The host is an in-process library The host is a library linked into the `morphir` binary. The CLI is a client of that library. This design has no separate host program. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph bin["morphir binary (one process)"] CLI["CLI client
args, files, cache, output"] HL["Host library
discovery, request, MEP"] CLI -->|function call| HL end HL <-->|MEP| Guest["guest
(Elm, Gleam, ...)"] ``` For `morphir compile src/Foo.elm --package-name My.Package`, the CLI passes the files, the language, and the package name. The library discovers the project, builds the protocol request, and talks to the guest. The CLI writes the result and prints the diagnostics. The CLI keeps output paths and the compile cache. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor User participant CLI as CLI client participant HL as Host library participant G as Elm guest User->>CLI: morphir compile src/Foo.elm --package-name My.Package CLI->>CLI: check compile cache CLI->>HL: compile(files, language = elm, package = My.Package, peer) HL->>HL: discover project, normalize name to my/package HL->>G: initialize, then compile request G-->>HL: IR and diagnostics HL-->>CLI: result CLI->>CLI: write IR to output path, update cache CLI-->>User: print diagnostics ``` The CLI tells the library its peer name and version. The library does not hardcode `morphir-cli`. ```rust // sketch let peer = PeerInfo { name: "morphir-cli".into(), version: env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION").into() }; ``` `ConnectedDaemonSession` remains a way to reach an extension over HTTP. The CLI does not use it to reach this library. Words for this thread: - **Host library.** The in-process library that discovers a project, builds the guest request, and talks to the guest. - **CLI client.** The `morphir` command. It parses arguments, calls the host library, writes files, and prints diagnostics. The next checkpoint names which operations the library exposes beside compile. ## Checkpoint 4. Compile, generate, and probe The host library exposes three operations: compile, generate, and probe. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph CLI["CLI client owns"] c1["compile: output paths, compile cache, config warnings"] c2["generate: find IR on disk, choose output dir, write files"] c3["install: copy files, update catalog"] end subgraph HL["Host library owns"] h1["compile: discover project, build request, call frontend guest"] h2["generate: select backend, call backend guest"] h3["probe: handshake, describe, check statement"] end c1 --> h1 c2 --> h2 c3 --> h3 HL --> V["one list of supported MEP versions
peer name and version from the client"] ``` For compile, the CLI passes the files, the language, and the package name. The library discovers the project, builds the protocol request, and talks to the guest. The CLI writes the result, prints the diagnostics, and keeps the output paths and the compile cache. For generate, the CLI finds the IR on disk and chooses the output directory. The library selects the backend and talks to the guest. The CLI writes the generated files. For probe, install still copies files and updates the catalog. It asks the library to probe the artifact. Compile, generate, and probe advertise the same supported protocol versions. The peer name and version still come from the CLI. ```rust // sketch host.compile(CompileInput { files, language, package_name }, &peer).await?; host.generate(GenerateInput { ir, target }, &peer).await?; host.probe(&artifact, &declared_statement, &peer).await?; ``` The next checkpoint decides whether a caller can keep a guest warm across many calls. The web workbench does that today, so a playground click does not spawn a new process each time. ## Checkpoint 5. Sessions are the core of the host library The host library gives clients a session. A session is one live guest after the handshake. Opening a session starts the guest, negotiates the protocol version, and stores the guest's capabilities. The session exposes compile, generate, and describe. The client owns the session's lifetime and closes it. A client can hold many sessions at the same time, one for each guest. A server can keep a few sessions for the same guest and use them like workers. The host library opens every guest. Guests do not connect back to the host. The host library has three layers. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph clients["Clients"] CLI["morphir compile / generate / install"] WB["web workbench"] SRV["server"] BR["browser (WASM + JS)"] end subgraph HL["Host library"] OS["One-shot helpers
compile, generate, probe"] POOL["Pool (optional)
reuse per key, evict dead guest, retry once"] S["Session
handshake, capabilities, compile, generate, describe"] OS --> S POOL --> S end CLI --> OS WB --> POOL SRV --> POOL SRV --> S BR --> S S --> T["transport
(later decision)"] ``` 1. **Session.** The core. `open(guest, peer)` returns a session. The peer name and version still come from the client. 2. **One-shot helpers.** Compile, generate, and probe each open a session, make one call, and close it. `morphir compile`, `morphir generate`, and install use these helpers. Probe opens a session, reads the capabilities, checks the statement, and closes the session. 3. **Pool.** An optional helper built on sessions. It keeps one guest for each key, removes a guest that stopped, and retries a request once on a new guest. This is the logic in `crates/morphir/src/commands/ui/provider/sessions.rs` today. The web workbench uses the pool instead of its own cache. A server can use the pool or build its own. ```rust // sketch pub struct Session { /* negotiated version, capabilities, transport */ } impl Session { pub async fn open(guest: GuestSpec, peer: PeerInfo) -> Result; pub fn capabilities(&self) -> &Capabilities; pub async fn compile(&mut self, request: CompileRequest) -> Result; pub async fn generate(&mut self, request: GenerateRequest) -> Result; pub async fn describe(&mut self) -> Result; pub async fn close(self) -> Result<()>; } // One-shot helper: open, call, close. pub async fn compile_once(guest: GuestSpec, peer: PeerInfo, request: CompileRequest) -> Result { let mut session = Session::open(guest, peer).await?; let result = session.compile(request).await; session.close().await?; result } // Optional pool. The client picks the key and the limits. pub struct Pool { /* K -> Session */ } impl Pool { pub async fn compile(&self, key: K, request: CompileRequest) -> Result; pub async fn generate(&self, key: K, request: GenerateRequest) -> Result; pub async fn abandon(&self, key: &K); } ``` Two playground clicks through the pool: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor User participant WB as Web workbench participant P as Pool participant S as Session participant G as Elm guest User->>WB: click Compile WB->>P: compile(key = elm, request) P->>S: open (no session yet for key) S->>G: start, initialize P->>S: compile S->>G: compile G-->>WB: IR User->>WB: click Generate WB->>P: generate(key = elm, request) P->>S: generate (same session, no start) S->>G: generate G-->>WB: files Note over P,G: if the guest stopped: evict, open a new session, retry once ``` The host library keeps no hidden global state. The client decides pool size, idle time, and tenant limits. Reason: the host library must serve the CLI, desktop and server clients, and browser clients through WASM with JS glue. A hidden pool needs global state and timers, and `wasm32` does not supply threads for them. A session handle maps to a JS object that the caller frees. It also gives a server control of concurrency and isolation. ```ts // sketch: browser client through a wasm-bindgen adapter using session = await Session.open(guest, { name: "morphir-web", version }); const result = await session.compile(request); // `using` calls session[Symbol.dispose]() here, which frees the guest. ``` Consequence: the session must not depend on one transport. Process stdio, Extism, HTTP, and a browser worker or in-page WASM guest must all fit behind the same session. The transport design is a later decision. ## Checkpoint 6. `morphir-host` crate and the WASM component model goal The host library lives in a new crate, `morphir-host`, in `finos/morphir-rust`. `morphir-host` is a portable core. Published contracts carry no prerelease tags. - A breaking change bumps the minor version: `0.2.x` to `0.3.0`. - An additive, backward-compatible change bumps the patch version: `0.2.1` to `0.2.2`. `@since(version = 0.2.2)` marks the new WIT items. - The JSON-RPC handshake sends the canonical version, for example `"0.2"`. Reason: WIT accepts full SemVer 2.0, prerelease included. The component model Explainer turns each version into a canonical version, and a host matches imports on that string. A version with a prerelease tag is never split, so each draft is a separate contract that needs an exact match. ```text 0.2.6 -> 0.2 (0.x: split after minor) 1.2.3 -> 1 (>= 1: split after major) 0.2.0-draft.1 -> 0.2.0-draft.1 (prerelease: never split) ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph A["minor-bump rule"] g1["guest imports morphir:mep@0.2.6"] -->|"canonical 0.2"| h1["host provides morphir:mep@0.2.1"] end subgraph B["prerelease tags"] g2["guest imports 0.2.0-draft.2"] -.-x|"no match"| h2["host provides 0.2.0-draft.1"] end ``` With the minor-bump rule, the JSON-RPC and WIT bindings negotiate and link the same way. title: Windows: morphir CLI needs MSVC Spectre-mitigated CRT libs to build (GH #886)
description:
cargo build -p morphir fails on a Windows host whose Visual Studio install lacks the Spectre-mitigated CRT libs, blocking build, test and clippy for the whole crate.

Chain: morphir -> morphir-opa -> regorus (std feature) -> msvc_spectre_libs with features = ["error"], whose build script panics rather than warns when the libs are absent. Introduced by 826f47c0, which added regorus and morphir-opa. Linux CI is unaffected, so only Windows contributors hit it.

Options: document the required VS component; raise it with regorus upstream (the "error" feature is opt-in, a warning is the crate default); make morphir-opa optional behind a feature.

Found while verifying GH #885 locally. Full analysis in GH #886.

comments.author: Damian Reeves
comments.text: Decision 2026-09-18 (Damian Reeves): two contracts, two owners. (1) 'My extension works with the released CLI' belongs to the extension repo (finos/morphir-rust#172). (2) 'A CLI change does not break bundles users already installed' belongs to finos/morphir, because request construction lives in crates/morphir and no extension repo sees a CLI PR. Evidence: all three faults found in the v0.4.0-beta.1 release verification were of kind 2 (python v0.1.0 missing exposedModules, elm-native irVersion 4.0.0, bare relative repository init) and CI missed them because it builds guests from the pinned submodule source, a pair no user has. Action: remove the WASM guest builds and the source-built guest tests from finos/morphir CI. Replace them with a consumer check that downloads published bundles at tags pinned in a file and runs python_extension, rust_extension, generate_extension and generate_openapi_extension with the CLI built from the PR. A deliberate protocol break must publish a compatible bundle first and move the pinned tag in the same CLI PR. The built-in morphir-elm-native provider is compiled into the CLI, so finos/morphir owns its check fully. Elm and Scala process extension builds stay until morphir-xgd9.10 is resolved.

design:
# IR ingestion contract audit

Follow-up to #790.

## Purpose

Run one deliberate, read-only review of every supported or specified Morphir IR
ingestion route through the normalized UI AST and the Insight and XRay views.
The review must produce one complete support matrix and one consolidated
findings report. It must not fix findings or trigger another PR-bot review.

This corrects a gap in the XRay review process. The implementation reviews were
organized around small commit ranges and individual acceptance slices. The
exhaustive semantic fixture covered V3, while the V4 smoke project exercised
only a few expanded forms. As a result, the reviews proved renderer coverage
and a narrow V4 happy path, but not representation parity across the V4 schema
or across storage layouts.

## Prior review history and mandatory regression anchors

The audit must retain and independently re-prove every prior PR #790 review
finding. A finding marked fixed is a regression anchor, not a row to skip:

- Codex review `5103345835`, inline comment `3925698261`: a fresh clone could
  not run the documented mise setup before trusting `.config/mise/config.toml`.
  Addressed by parent commits `ef584982` and `41db85f4`. This is outside the IR
  semantic matrix but remains a checkout/setup precondition for the audit.
- Codex review `5103916579`: nested tuple patterns and subjects produced
  misaligned Insight decision-table columns. Addressed in morphir-ui commits
  `887d95c`, `050322f`, `e822422`, and `8b785e7`, vendored by parent commit
  `298e00ce`. Re-prove recursive, opaque, opposing, and arity-mismatch cases.
- Codex review `5104505026`: exact baseline release string `4.0.0` was rejected,

  by parent commit `d121e9bd`. Re-prove all schema-listed access spellings and

Preserve these deliberate exclusions and unresolved contexts:

  `4.1.0`. The current exact-release policy recognizes later release strings

## Scope

Audit these input profiles:

1. V3 single-file JSON
2. V3 single-file YAML
3. V4 single-file JSON
4. V4 single-file YAML
5. V4 JSON document tree/VFS
6. V4 YAML document tree/VFS

For each applicable profile, follow both entry paths:

- browser file or folder loading;
- connected `morphir live` workspace loading.

Trace each route through parsing/loading, normalization into the shared AST,
definition selection, Insight transformation/rendering, and XRay
projection/rendering. A route that is specified but not implemented is a
product capability gap, not automatically a decoder defect.

The audit covers every schema-defined type expression, pattern, literal, and
value expression, including accepted compact and expanded spellings, access
wrappers, documentation, attributes, recursive nesting, and malformed or
future-compatible fallback behavior. V3/V4 semantic equivalents must normalize
to equivalent ASTs. JSON/YAML and single-file/document-tree storage choices
must not change the rendered semantic result.

The audit excludes unrelated CLI serving, deployment, performance,
observability, and multi-user production hardening.

## Normative sources and implementation boundaries

Treat these as normative or contract-defining inputs:

- `website/static/schemas/morphir-ir-v3.json`
- `website/static/schemas/morphir-ir-v4.json`

- `crates/morphir/src/commands/ui/`

Use existing tests and fixtures as evidence, but do not treat their existence or

## Deliverables and stop rule

Produce:

1. A representation matrix with a row for every schema-defined alternative and
   columns for all applicable input profiles and entry paths. Each cell must be
   `supported`, `rejected with diagnostic`, `degrades to unknown`, `not
   implemented`, or `not applicable`, with evidence.
2. One ranked findings report. Every finding must cite the schema/contract,
   source location, minimal reproduction, observed result, expected result, and
   affected matrix cells.
3. A short gap summary grouped as code defect, missing product capability,
   fixture/spec inconsistency, or test-only gap.
4. A proposed issue breakdown that keeps delivery blockers separate from
   optional hardening.

Do not edit source, add tests, create fix commits, request GitHub reviews, or
stop after the first valid finding. Complete the matrix and report all findings
in one pass. Implementation begins only after maintainers review and prioritize
the consolidated report.

## Reusable review prompt

```text
Perform a deliberate, read-only contract audit of Morphir IR ingestion through
the web UI. This is not a diff review and not a request to fix code. Review the
whole contract boundary once, then return one consolidated report. Do not stop
after the first finding and do not request another reviewer.

Goal
Prove whether semantically equivalent Morphir IR reaches equivalent normalized
ASTs and remains usable in both Insight and XRay across:

- V3 single-file JSON
- V3 single-file YAML
- V4 single-file JSON
- V4 single-file YAML
- V4 JSON document tree/VFS
- V4 YAML document tree/VFS

Exercise both browser file/folder loading and connected `morphir live`
workspace loading wherever applicable. Document-tree layouts are V4-only.

Sources of truth
Read the relevant AGENTS.md files first. Then use:

- website/static/schemas/morphir-ir-v3.json
- website/static/schemas/morphir-ir-v4.json
- website/static/schemas/morphir-ir-v4-document-tree-files.json

- ecosystem/morphir-ui/apps/morphir-web/src/connected/connected-provider.ts
- ecosystem/morphir-ui/packages/morphir-ir/src/{decode,ast-decode,names,ast}.ts
- ecosystem/morphir-ui/packages/morphir-insight/src/
- ecosystem/morphir-ui/packages/morphir-ui/src/views/insight/

Audit method

1. Reconcile PR #790 review history first. Re-prove review IDs `5103345835`,
   `5103916579`, `5104505026`, and `5105072844` against the current source and
   record each as passing, regressed, deliberately excluded, or superseded.
2. Inventory every schema-defined alternative before evaluating support:
   envelope/release spellings; distribution and module shapes; access wrappers;
   docs and attributes; names, paths, and FQNames; all type expressions; all
   patterns; all literals; all value expressions; inline and granular
   document-tree definitions.
3. For every alternative, enumerate compact, expanded, legacy-compatible, and
   recursive forms that the schema explicitly accepts. Do not infer support
   from one representative example.
4. Build a matrix across the six profiles and two entry paths. Mark each cell
   only as: supported; rejected with diagnostic; degrades to unknown; not
   implemented; or not applicable. Cite a test, controlled probe, or direct
   source trace for every non-obvious result.
5. Validate cross-profile invariants: equivalent JSON and YAML, and equivalent
   single-file and document-tree inputs, must normalize to equivalent ASTs and
   render the same selected definition in Insight and XRay.
6. Verify that every valid semantic node reaches the shared AST without an
   UnknownNode, omission, crash, or data loss, and that Insight/XRay handle every
   normalized kind. Verify unknown future tags degrade safely.
7. Probe malformed boundaries: nulls, arrays where maps are required, missing
   required fields, ambiguous access wrappers or manifests, mixed serialization

   decoder calls, unsupported versions, and size/path confinement already
   promised by the loaders. Use only trusted local fixtures and controlled
   values.
8. Run the relevant existing tests, but do not treat green tests as coverage.
   Identify matrix rows with no executable evidence.

Classification

- Code defect: a currently supported route violates its schema or loses,
  misnormalizes, or misrenders valid IR.
- Missing product capability: a specified/desired route has no complete loader
  path to Insight/XRay (for example, a loader stops at document-tree metadata).
- Fixture/spec inconsistency: published examples or fixtures violate the
  normative contract.
- Test-only gap: behavior is correct by source trace and probe but lacks durable

Report format

1. Findings first, ranked Critical, Important, Minor. For each finding include:

2. The complete representation matrix, including unsupported and untested

5. Proposed follow-up issues grouped into delivery blockers and optional
   hardening. Avoid unrelated refactors or productionization.
6. Commands/probes run and their results.

Stop after the consolidated report. Do not edit code, add tests, commit, push,
comment on a PR, or trigger a bot review.
```

title: Playground: reuse a daemon session via SessionHandle instead of a cold invocation per compile
description:
Every Playground compile and generate currently starts a fresh extension invocation. The Kameo SessionActor that makes reuse possible landed on morphir-rust main (PR #142), but the CLI's NativePlaygroundProvider in crates/morphir/src/commands/ui/provider/playground.rs does not hold a SessionHandle yet, so nothing benefits from it.

Wiring it through means a compile pays extension startup once per session rather than once per click. That is also the precondition for the interaction the try-morphir experience implies: compiling on a debounce as the user types is only defensible once a compile stops spawning a process, which is why the current view deliberately compiles on explicit click only (see the comment on compile() in PlaygroundView.svelte).

Scope: hold a session per (provider, language) in the provider, route compile/generate through it, and honor DaemonError::SessionLost by evicting and respawning rather than surfacing the error.
close_reason: Shipped in finos/morphir#783 (3147cd41). SessionReuseInvoker holds one SessionHandle per provider id, keyed within that by provider incarnation (version/origin/invocation mode) so an upgrade mid-run does not keep serving the old binary. SessionLost evicts and retries once; a rejection keeps the session; a playground timeout calls the new ExtensionInvoker::abandon so a wedged actor is not left cached; native-direct falls through to the unchanged one-shot path. Also bumped the morphir-rust pin to 60cc88b, which the CLI needed before SessionHandle was reachable at all.

title: Playground: prefer an IR version the client can decode when the frontend offers a choice
description:
preferredIrVersion in morphir-ui packages/morphir-ui/src/views/playground/playground-state.svelte.ts picks the frontend's first advertised IR version whenever no target agreement narrows the choice. Nothing in that pick consults what @morphir/ir can actually decode (decode.ts hard-rejects any formatVersion other than 3), so a frontend advertising both 4 and 3 with 4 listed first yields a compile whose IR the Insight and XRay panes cannot render, even though asking for 3 would have rendered fine. The compile itself succeeds, which makes the failure look like a bug in the views rather than in the request.

Fix: among the versions that satisfy the chosen target (generation compatibility stays non-negotiable), prefer one this client can decode, and fall back to the first candidate when none is decodable so compile and generate still work and only the visualization degrades. The decodable set belongs to @morphir/ir as a single source of truth so the Playground follows automatically when v4 decoding lands.

Note the wire spells versions inconsistently: providers advertise both a bare major ('3') and a full triplet ('4.0.0'), so the match is on the major component.

Related: morphir-19s6 covers making v4 renderable at all; this issue is about not asking for an unrenderable version when a renderable one was on offer.
close_reason: Fixed in morphir-ui#29 (0910e8aa); vendored into the CLI by finos/morphir#781. preferredIrVersion now prefers a decodable IR version among those the chosen target agrees to, with DECODABLE_FORMAT_VERSIONS in @morphir/ir as the single source of truth so the predicate and decodeMorphirIr cannot drift.

title: Playground provider: contain extension output in a scratch directory instead of blocklisting options
description:
The connected Playground must never write into the user's workspace, and today that invariant is enforced by deny_output_options in crates/morphir/src/commands/ui/provider/playground.rs: it strips outputDir and pins emitParseStage=false before invoking a backend. That is a blocklist, so it only holds for the option names known when it was written. A new extension option that writes to disk, or a provider that ignores the pinned value, defeats it silently, and the failure mode is files appearing in a workspace the user never asked to modify.

Replace it with containment: run the invocation in a scratch directory the host owns, and treat a write outside it as the extension's problem rather than the host's. Artifacts already come back in-band over MEP, so nothing the Playground needs depends on where the extension writes.

Acceptance: the no-write invariant holds for an extension requesting an output path the host has never seen, proven by a test that invokes a backend with an unknown write-shaped option and asserts the workspace is untouched.

title: Git hooks are dormant in this clone: EasyCLA AI-trailer guard never runs
description:
package.json declares 'prepare: husky' and .husky/ contains commit-msg, pre-commit and pre-push hooks, but none of them execute: core.hooksPath is unset and .git/hooks contains only samples. husky was never installed in this clone.

What is not running:
- commit-msg, which strips Co-Authored-By trailers naming AI assistants. This is the EasyCLA compliance guard that CLAUDE.md calls critical, and it is currently unenforced - compliance depends entirely on the author remembering.
- pre-commit, which blocks committing .beads as a symlink from a worktree.
- pre-push, which runs fmt-check, lint and test.

Enabling them is not a clean 'npm install': the pre-push hook checks Go formatting ('Checking Go formatting...' then 'mise run fmt-check'), which looks like leftover text from the morphir-go template. Turning hooks on would start gating every push on tasks that may not be right for this repo, so the pre-push body should be reviewed before activation.

Suggested order: correct pre-push for this repository, then activate hooks, then confirm the commit-msg guard actually strips a test trailer.
close_reason: Activated the hooks and corrected pre-push. Root cause was that activation depended on husky's npm prepare script, which never runs in a cargo/bun/mise repository, so core.hooksPath stayed unset in every clone. Added tools/install-git-hooks.ts to set core.hooksPath to .husky without needing node, exposed as mise run hooks:install and hooks:check, and made mise run init depend on it so a normal setup activates hooks. Wired it as a dependency rather than into the init body so it also runs on Windows without POSIX bash. Found and fixed a second reason the hooks would not have run even once activated: all three were mode 100644 in the index, and git silently skips non-executable hooks on Linux and macOS; they are now 100755. Rewrote pre-push, which claimed to check Go formatting and ran cargo clippy --all-targets plus cargo test --workspace, taking many minutes and not linking on some machines; it now runs mise run fmt-check only, measured at 1.6s, with a MORPHIR_SKIP_HOOKS=1 escape hatch, on the reasoning that CI already gates lint and tests and a hook slow enough to be bypassed protects nothing. title: beads: DB and git-tracked export drift because jsonl edits bypass Dolt
description:
Reconciled on 2026-08-30: the Dolt DB and .beads/issues.jsonl had drifted in both directions - 17 issues existed only in the DB, morphir-0ley existed only in the jsonl, and 5 issues disagreed on status.

Root cause, two independent mechanisms:

1. Commit 7a211a47 (PR #739) wrote beads changes into .beads/issues.jsonl and committed them to git without a corresponding 'bd dolt push'. Both jsonl-only facts came from that one commit: morphir-0ley was created and morphir-l2p9.2 was closed, and the DB never learned either. AGENTS.md line 374 states the intended model - the DB is authoritative, sync travels over refs/dolt/data, and the jsonl is a passive export - so hand-editing the export is the documented anti-pattern. Nothing enforces it.

2. Issues created through bd were committed to Dolt but never re-exported into the git-tracked jsonl, leaving 17 DB-only records.

Amplifier: bd resolves .beads to the main checkout (C:/Users/damre/code/repos/github/finos/morphir/.beads) even when the cwd is a linked worktree. Work done in a worktree edits that worktree's tracked jsonl, while bd reads and writes the main checkout's copy. When the main checkout is behind origin/main (it was by 8 commits), bd's view of the export is stale.

Resolution applied: imported the two jsonl-authoritative records into the DB, then exported the DB over the tracked jsonl. Conflicts were resolved by updated_at - the DB was newer for the 4 h0pf records, the jsonl was newer for l2p9.2. Verified afterwards: 301 issues on both sides, no id present on only one side, no status or priority disagreement, no ids lost.

Prevention to decide on:
- 'bd hooks install' would chain DB and export automatically, but this clone has no active git hooks at all (see the separate finding about dormant husky hooks), so installing bd shims needs care about what else they chain to.
- A cheaper option is a drift check in the 'check' mise task: bd export to a temp file and diff ids and statuses against .beads/issues.jsonl, failing when they disagree.
- Either way the worktree and main-checkout .beads split should be documented in AGENTS.md, since it silently makes bd operate on a different file than the one being committed.

Also worth fixing: bd export orders the dependencies array non-deterministically, so re-exporting an unchanged issue produces a spurious diff. That churn hides real changes in review - 16 records showed as modified when only 5 had actually changed.
close_reason: Added a drift check and wired it into the commit path. tools/check-beads-drift.ts compares bd export against .beads/issues.jsonl by id, status and priority, deliberately ignoring the dependencies array because bd emits its entries in a non-deterministic order that produces diff churn without meaning disagreement. Exposed as mise run beads:drift-check, and the pre-commit hook runs it when .beads/issues.jsonl is staged, which is the moment the drift would be introduced. Verified against all three drift kinds by injecting each into a copy of the export: an issue only in the database, an issue only in the export, and a status disagreement, all detected, then confirmed a real commit with a drifted export is blocked while an in-sync one passes. Documented the invariant in AGENTS.md along with the worktree gotcha that bd resolves .beads to the main checkout even when the cwd is a linked worktree. The drift that prompted this was already reconciled in PR #748.

title: morphir ir migrate: --path-budget writer option for the portable profile
description: The v4 format defines pathBudget (default 4000, portable profile 200) and the spec says every manifest records the budget it was written with. But the writer cannot be told to use anything except the default: crates/morphir/src/commands/migrate.rs write_tree() builds CodecOptions::new(version, layout, format) with no budget parameter, and CodecOptions/DocumentTreeSink in ecosystem/morphir-rust carry none either. Editing pathBudget in an already-written manifest only relabels filenames chosen under the default. Needed: plumb a path budget through CodecOptions and the document-tree sink in morphir-rust (truncation via to_file_stem + fileNames map already exists), expose it as --path-budget on morphir ir migrate here, and record the value in the emitted manifest. Surfaced by Codex review on PR #747; docs/getting-started/morphir-cli.md now marks the portable profile as not yet writable by the CLI. Related: morphir-zz6f (doctor should report budget/machine mismatches).

title: morphir doctor: diagnose long path support and path budget
description:
Add a `morphir doctor` command that checks the local environment and reports what would break, starting with the long path handling that the IR v4 path budget depends on.

Checks it should make:
- git core.longpaths, which Git for Windows ships off, so a checkout fails past 260 characters even when Windows allows long paths
- the Windows LongPathsEnabled registry value under HKLM SYSTEM CurrentControlSet Control FileSystem
- whether the running process is longPathAware, since the registry setting alone does not help a process without the manifest declaration
- the effective usable path length, probed rather than inferred
- for a document tree in scope: the pathBudget recorded in its manifest against what this machine can actually open, and any path over 260 characters in a tree written under the long budget

It should offer the remediation rather than only naming the problem, and should exit non-zero when a tree in scope cannot be read on this machine.

Context: kb decision 0001 flips the default path budget to 4000 and requires pathBudget to be recorded in every manifest, precisely so a reader can report a mismatch up front instead of failing file by file. doctor is where that report belongs. Guidance currently lives in AGENTS.md and in the mise init task warning.

No doctor command exists yet; crates/morphir/src/commands/ has no such module.

title: v4 schema has diverged from the published v4 examples
description:
mise run examples:validate fails on the v4 examples. Pre-existing: both failed identically against the schema as committed before the naming branch.

RESOLVED so far:
- AccessControlled accepted only {Public:...} or {access,value}, not the flattened {access, TypeAliasDefinition} form the document tree spec documents and every example uses. Fixed by adding a branch and switching oneOf to anyOf.
- OpaqueTypeSpecification had an inner oneOf whose second branch (object with only "annotations") was a strict subset of the first, so any matching value matched both and "exactly one" never held. That rejected { "OpaqueTypeSpecification": {} }, the canonical form the definition documents and gives as its first example. Fixed by collapsing to one schema. books-and-records-example.json now validates.

REMAINING, and it is a design decision rather than a typo. complete-example.json encodes a parameterized type reference as a bare array:

  "typeExp": ["morphir/sdk:list#list", "a"]

Two parts of the specification disagree about what that means:
- morphir-ir-v4.yaml: TupleType accepts bare arrays *specifically because* ReferenceType does not. Its own comment reads "Unambiguous because ReferenceType does not accept bare arrays." Under this reading the value above is a 2-element Tuple.
- docs/spec/ir/schemas/v4/document-tree-files.md tells authors: "Array format: [\"morphir/SDK:list#list\", \"my-org/domain:types#user\"] (for parameterized types) ... the first element is the type constructor and subsequent elements are type arguments." Under this reading it is a parameterized Reference.

These are mutually exclusive and the difference changes what the IR means, not just whether it validates. Someone has to decide which reading is canonical, then align the other side and the examples. If Reference gains a bare-array form, the ambiguity with Tuple has to be resolved some other way.

complete-example.json also uses legacy tagged arrays for function types, e.g. "f": ["Function", {}, "a", "b"], which needs the same decision about whether v4 accepts them.
close_reason: Resolved by decision A: a bare array is a Tuple, a parameterized reference uses the Reference wrapper. Fixed AccessControlled flattened form, the OpaqueTypeSpecification overlapping oneOf, the spec page's array-format note, and rewrote both v4 examples (9 sites, incl. legacy Function and ad-hoc Tuple tags). examples:validate passes: 6 files, 0 errors.

Findings: src/data.rs is headed 'Sample data for demonstration purposes'; morphir_core is a declared dependency but imported nowhere in src/; all three settings save paths are '// TODO: Actually save the config' (pages/project_settings.rs:32, components/layout.rs:438, pages/workspace_settings.rs:26); zero tests; components/detail_views/* duplicates components/pages/* and layout.rs still carries a ViewState rendering path parallel to the router. title: Lint generated CLI docs for MDX-hostile characters

title: Establish durable formatVersion contract from v3 onward
description: Define and deliver one formatVersion contract beginning with IR v3 and inherited by every later major family. Preserve integer aliases, add exact release strings, reject unsupported exact versions before semantic decoding, keep JSON and YAML member order semantically irrelevant, canonicalize formatVersion first, expose replay-cost lint observations, and align the parent specification with Rust, Scala, and Elm implementations.
acceptance_criteria: V1 and v2 remain integer-only. For every major N at or above 3, integer N normalizes to N.0.0 and strict N.minor.patch strings retain exact revisions. Readers reject unsupported exact versions with stable diagnostics before semantic callbacks. Canonical JSON and YAML place formatVersion first while readers accept either root order with bounded memory. Overflow never wraps. Parent schemas and conformance fixtures, Rust transport and CLI behavior, Scala intent and codecs, and Elm codecs implement the shared contract with repository quality gates passing.
notes:
Agreed design direction: JSON and YAML root member order remains semantically irrelevant. Canonical writers emit formatVersion first. Linting warns when distribution precedes formatVersion, with stronger guidance when the late key forces a full scan for a large IR. FormatVersion uses one permanent contract beginning with major version 3 and applying to every later major family: integer N aliases exactly N.0.0, while strict release strings N.minor.patch preserve later revisions. V1 and V2 remain integer-only historical profiles. Each reader recognizes future major families and same-major revisions but normalizes only exact versions it explicitly declares supported; otherwise it returns a stable unsupported-version diagnostic, preventing silent lossy reads. The contract must align parent specs and schemas, morphir-rust codecs and CLI diagnostics, and ecosystem intent and implementations including morphir-scala and morphir-elm.

title: Implement design-time extension runtime
description:
Implement the runtime interface for design-time extensions (frontend, backend, common-backend) using the process() pattern.

## Background
Design-time extensions transform Morphir IR or source code. They use a simpler call pattern than runtime extensions: process(input) -> output.

## Tasks
- [ ] Implement DesignTimeExtension trait with process() method
- [ ] Add support for frontend-compile(input: Envelope) -> Envelope
- [ ] Add support for backend-generate(input: Envelope) -> Envelope
- [ ] Add support for get-capabilities() -> Envelope
- [ ] Implement extension registry for discovery
- [ ] Add configuration-driven extension loading
- [ ] Handle design-time specific host functions (workspace, ir_helpers)

## Acceptance Criteria
- DesignTimeExtension can load and call frontend extensions
- DesignTimeExtension can load and call backend extensions
- Extension registry discovers extensions from config
- Capabilities querying works correctly
- Design-time host functions are available to extensions

## References
- docs/contributors/design/extensions/actor-based/12-wasm-extension-architecture-session.md (lines 383-508)

## Related Issues
- Depends on: morphir-rust-ext1
- Part of WASM extension architecture (see morphir-rust-kw8)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Error handling is robust and informative

title: Design and implement Morphir daemon and extension system
description:
Design and implement a complete Morphir daemon and extension system, enabling long-running services, IDE integration, and pluggable language/backend support.

## Vision

Create a daemon-based architecture that:
1. Provides fast, incremental compilation through persistent state
2. Enables IDE extensions (VS Code, IntelliJ, etc.) via LSP
3. Supports pluggable frontends (language bindings) and backends (code generators)
4. Offers real-time validation and type checking

---

## Phase 1: MVP Daemon (P1)

### Goals
- Basic daemon process that stays running
- Unix socket or TCP communication
- Simple request/response protocol (JSON-RPC or custom)
- File watching for automatic recompilation

### Deliverables
- `morphir-daemon` crate with basic lifecycle management
- `morphir daemon start/stop/status` CLI commands
- Simple compile request handling
- Basic health check endpoint

### Architecture
```
┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐
│  CLI/IDE    │────▶│  Morphir Daemon │
└─────────────┘     │  ┌───────────┐  │
                    │  │  Compiler │  │
                    │  └───────────┘  │
                    │  ┌───────────┐  │
                    │  │  Cache    │  │
                    │  └───────────┘  │
                    └─────────────────┘
```

---

## Phase 2: Extension System Design (P1)

### Goals
- Define extension API and plugin interface
- Support dynamic loading of language bindings
- Support dynamic loading of code generators
- Configuration-driven extension discovery

### Extension Types
1. **Frontend Extensions** (Language Bindings)
   - Parse source language → Morphir IR
   - Examples: Gleam, Python, TypeScript, Elm

2. **Backend Extensions** (Code Generators)
   - Morphir IR → Target language/platform
   - Examples: Spark, Flink, SQL, JavaScript

3. **Analyzer Extensions**
   - Custom validation rules
   - Type inference plugins
   - Documentation generators

### Plugin Interface
```rust
pub trait FrontendExtension {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    fn file_extensions(&self) -> &[&str];
    fn parse(&self, source: &str) -> Result<ModuleIR>;
}

pub trait BackendExtension {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    fn generate(&self, ir: &Distribution) -> Result<GeneratedOutput>;
}
```

---

## Phase 3: LSP Implementation (P2)

### Goals
- Language Server Protocol implementation
- Real-time diagnostics and error reporting
- Go-to-definition, find references
- Hover information with type details
- Code completion suggestions

### Deliverables
- `morphir-lsp` crate
- VS Code extension package
- Support for multiple source languages

---

## Phase 4: Production Hardening (P2)

### Goals
- Robust error handling and recovery
- Graceful shutdown and restart
- Logging and observability (tracing, metrics)
- Resource limits and throttling
- Multi-project workspace support

### Deliverables
- Structured logging with tracing
- Prometheus metrics endpoint
- Watchdog and auto-restart
- Connection pooling and request queuing

---

## Phase 5: IDE Extensions (P3)

### Goals
- VS Code extension with full feature set
- IntelliJ plugin
- Neovim/Vim LSP configuration
- Emacs support

### Features
- Syntax highlighting
- Inline error display
- Code actions and quick fixes
- Morphir IR visualization
- Type hierarchy explorer

---

## Implementation Approach

### Incremental Delivery
1. Start with MVP daemon (file watch + compile)
2. Add extension loading mechanism
3. Implement LSP basics (diagnostics)
4. Expand LSP features iteratively
5. Build IDE extensions on stable LSP

### Technology Choices
- **IPC**: Unix sockets (local), TCP (remote)
- **Protocol**: JSON-RPC 2.0 (LSP compatible)
- **Plugin Loading**: Dynamic libraries or WASM
- **File Watching**: notify crate

---

## Success Criteria

### MVP
- [ ] Daemon starts and accepts connections
- [ ] File changes trigger recompilation
- [ ] Compilation results returned to client
- [ ] Clean shutdown on signal

### Extension System
- [ ] Extensions discovered from config
- [ ] Dynamic loading works
- [ ] Multiple frontends can coexist
- [ ] Multiple backends can coexist

### LSP
- [ ] Diagnostics appear in VS Code
- [ ] Go-to-definition works
- [ ] Type information on hover
- [ ] Extension published to marketplace

---

## Related Issues
- morphir-cet: Switch to official Gleam parser (frontend extension)
- morphir-rust-72s: Python binding using Ruff (frontend extension)
- morphir-rust-ykr: TypeScript binding using SWC (frontend extension)

title: Implement TypeScript binding using SWC parser crate
description:
Create a morphir-typescript-binding crate that uses SWC's parser and AST crates to parse TypeScript source code and convert it to Morphir IR.

## Background

SWC (Speedy Web Compiler) is a fast TypeScript/JavaScript compiler written in Rust. It provides production-quality parser and AST crates:
- `swc_ecma_parser` - ECMAScript/TypeScript parser
- `swc_ecma_ast` - ECMAScript/TypeScript AST types

## Goals

1. Create `morphir-typescript-binding` crate following the same pattern as `morphir-gleam-binding`
2. Use SWC's parser crate for parsing TypeScript source files
3. Transform SWC's TypeScript AST to Morphir IR
4. Leverage TypeScript's type annotations for rich type information
5. Enable roundtrip testing (TypeScript → IR → TypeScript)

## Benefits

- **Performance**: SWC is one of the fastest TS/JS parsers available
- **Correctness**: Battle-tested parser used by Next.js, Deno, and other major projects
- **Compatibility**: Full TypeScript syntax support including latest features
- **Maintenance**: Active development with regular releases

## Implementation Steps

1. Add swc_ecma_parser and swc_ecma_ast as dependencies
2. Create TypeScript AST to ModuleIR visitor
3. Handle TypeScript-specific constructs (interfaces, type aliases, generics)
4. Support both .ts and .tsx files
5. Add BDD acceptance tests with TypeScript fixtures
6. Support TypeScript project parsing (tsconfig.json awareness)

## TypeScript Features to Support

- Function declarations with type annotations
- Interface and type alias definitions
- Class definitions
- Module imports/exports
- Generic types
- Union and intersection types

## References

- SWC GitHub: https://github.com/swc-project/swc
- swc_ecma_parser crate: https://crates.io/crates/swc_ecma_parser
- swc_ecma_ast crate: https://crates.io/crates/swc_ecma_ast

title: Implement Python binding using Ruff parser crate
description:
Create a morphir-python-binding crate that uses Ruff's parser and AST crates to parse Python source code and convert it to Morphir IR.

## Background

Ruff is a fast Python linter and formatter written in Rust. It provides high-quality parser and AST crates that can be reused:
- `ruff_python_parser` - Python parser
- `ruff_python_ast` - Python AST types

## Goals

1. Create `morphir-python-binding` crate following the same pattern as `morphir-gleam-binding`
2. Use Ruff's parser crate for parsing Python source files
3. Transform Ruff's Python AST to Morphir IR
4. Support Python type hints for type information extraction
5. Enable roundtrip testing (Python → IR → Python)

## Benefits

- **Performance**: Ruff's parser is highly optimized Rust code
- **Correctness**: Well-tested parser used in production by the Ruff project
- **Compatibility**: Supports modern Python syntax (3.7+)
- **Maintenance**: Parser updates come from active Ruff development

## Implementation Steps

1. Add ruff_python_parser and ruff_python_ast as dependencies
2. Create Python AST to ModuleIR visitor
3. Implement type annotation parsing for function signatures
4. Add BDD acceptance tests with Python fixtures
5. Support Python project parsing (multiple modules)

## References

- Ruff GitHub: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff
- ruff_python_parser crate: https://crates.io/crates/ruff_python_parser
- ruff_python_ast crate: https://crates.io/crates/ruff_python_ast
notes: Python ADTs, conditionals, fixed tuples, arbitrary precision integers, native/WASM frontend and backend, release packaging and documented support limits delivered. title: Fix failing Gleam binding acceptance tests
description:
Several Gleam binding acceptance tests are failing and have been marked as @wip (work in progress):

## Failing Tests

### 1. Roundtrip Tests (roundtrip.feature)
- **order_validation** scenario - Parser fails on generated function signatures with tupled arguments
- **order_processing** scenario - Same parser issue with function signatures

### 2. CLI Integration Tests (cli.feature)
- All CLI tests - Require full CLI functionality to be implemented

### 3. Project Parsing Tests (project.feature)
- Module name lookup uses full path instead of module name (e.g., looking for 'main' but stored as 'src/main')

### 4. Workspace Tests (workspace.feature)
- Workspace parsing not yet implemented

### 5. Code Generation Tests (codegen.feature)
- Code generation steps not yet implemented

## Root Causes

1. **Roundtrip failures**: The Gleam parser generates function signatures with tupled parameters like `fn(#(a, b))` but cannot parse them back. The signature should be `fn(a, b)` or handle tupled parameters correctly.

2. **Project parsing**: Module names need to be derived from the file path relative to src/, not include the full path or 'src/' prefix.

3. **CLI/Workspace/Codegen**: These features are not yet implemented.

## Impact
Blocking full roundtrip testing for complex business logic fixtures.

title: Morphir AssemblyScript Backend

## Goals
- Generate idiomatic AssemblyScript from Morphir IR

## Rationale
AssemblyScript provides a TypeScript-like developer experience while compiling to WebAssembly. This makes it an attractive target for:

- Debugging Wasm output (readable intermediate code)
- Prototyping before optimizing with lower-level backends

## Scope

- Value expression codegen
- Module structure generation
- Component Model boundary handling
- Runtime support library

title: Add CLI usage specs for workspace and compile commands
description:
## Context

The VFS protocol v4 design now includes comprehensive JSON-RPC methods for:
- Workspace management (create, open, close, projects, dependencies)
- Frontend compilation (workspace, project, module, files, fragment)
- VFS operations (read, propose, commit, subscribe)

## Format

Use **usage specs** (https://usage.jdx.dev/spec/) - KDL-based CLI specification format ("OpenAPI for CLIs").

Example structure:
```kdl
name "morphir"
bin "morphir"
version "4.0.0"
about "Morphir CLI - functional domain modeling toolchain"

cmd "workspace" help="Manage workspaces" {
    cmd "init" help="Create a new workspace" {
        arg "<path>" help="Workspace root directory"
        flag "-n --name <name>" help="Workspace name"
    }
    cmd "open" help="Open an existing workspace" {
        arg "<path>" help="Workspace root directory"
    }
    // ...
}

cmd "compile" help="Compile Morphir source to IR" {
    arg "[path]" help="Project or workspace path" default="."
    flag "-m --module <module>" help="Compile single module"
    flag "-i --incremental" help="Incremental compilation"
    flag "-w --watch" help="Watch for changes"
}
```

## Scope

Define usage specs for:

### Workspace Commands
- `morphir workspace init` - Create new workspace
- `morphir workspace open` - Open existing workspace  
- `morphir workspace close` - Close workspace
- `morphir workspace add` - Add project to workspace
- `morphir workspace remove` - Remove project
- `morphir workspace list` - List projects
- `morphir workspace build` - Build all projects
- `morphir workspace clean` - Clean artifacts
- `morphir workspace watch` - Watch for changes

### Compile Commands
- `morphir compile` - Compile project/workspace
- `morphir compile --module` - Compile single module
- `morphir compile --files` - Compile specific files
- `morphir compile --fragment` - Compile code fragment (REPL)

### Dependency Commands
- `morphir deps add` - Add dependency
- `morphir deps remove` - Remove dependency
- `morphir deps resolve` - Resolve dependencies
- `morphir deps list` - List dependencies

### Generate Commands
- `morphir generate` - Generate target code
- `morphir generate --target` - Specify target language

## Deliverables
- `morphir.usage.kdl` - Complete usage spec file
- Integration with shell completions (bash, zsh, fish)
- Man page generation
- Help text validation

title: Improve release process based on v0.4.0-alpha.2 retrospective
description:
## Context

During the v0.4.0-alpha.2 release, we encountered several issues that required 3 workflow attempts before success. This task tracks the recommended improvements from the post-release retrospective.

## Issues Encountered

1. **New modules without prior tags** - `pkg/bindings/golang` and `pkg/toolchain` were new but go.mod referenced v0.4.0-alpha.1
2. **Bash arithmetic bug** - `((var++))` returns 1 when incrementing from 0, causing early exit with `set -e`
3. **Missing setup-workspace in release workflow** - `go mod tidy` validates versions before applying replace directives

## Recommended Improvements

### 1. Update release-validate.sh

Add checks for:
- [ ] New modules without prior tags
- [ ] go.mod references to non-existent versions
- [ ] Simulate `go mod tidy` without go.work to catch issues early

```bash
# Add to release-validate.sh
rm -f go.work go.work.sum
bash ./scripts/remove-replace-directives.sh
go mod tidy -C cmd/morphir 2>&1 || echo "FAIL: go mod tidy would fail in release"
git checkout -- .  # Restore
```

### 2. Merge PR #544

The bash arithmetic fix in release-tags.sh (PR #544) should be merged.

### 3. Update release-manager skill

Add "Adding New Modules" section documenting:
- Create stub tags for new modules at prior version, OR
- Update go.mod references in same PR, OR
- Ensure setup-workspace handles the transition

### 4. Pre-release checklist additions

- [ ] Verify all new modules have tags or proper version references
- [ ] Run `goreleaser release --snapshot --clean` locally

## Related PRs

- #542 - Release prep
- #543 - Add setup-workspace to release workflow
- #544 - Fix release-tags.sh arithmetic (pending)
- #545 - Update internal module references

title: IR JSON Serialization: Configurable emission strategies
description:
Add foundational JSON/JSONL serialization support to pkg/models/ir with configurable emission strategies.

## Background
Currently IR types use unexported fields, requiring ad-hoc serialization in CLI code. JSON serialization should be a first-class capability in the models package.

## Requirements

### Configurable Emission Strategies
Support different JSON emission modes via configurable MarshalJSON:

1. **Full Distribution** (traditional)
   - Emit entire Morphir IR as single JSON document
   - Compatible with existing morphir-elm tooling

2. **JSONL Split Emission** (streaming/batch)
   - Emit modules/types/values as separate JSON lines
   - Enables streaming processing of large IRs
   - Better for incremental/parallel processing

3. **Package Emission**
   - Emit with package context/metadata
   - Include package namespace, name, version

4. **Distribution Metadata**
   - Emit distribution info (version, etc.) as own JSON line
   - Support header/footer metadata lines in JSONL mode

### Implementation Approach
- Add MarshalJSON methods to IR types (ModuleDefinition, Type, Value, etc.)
- Create EmitOptions/EmitConfig for controlling emission strategy
- Support both pretty JSON and compact JSONL
- Maintain compatibility with Morphir IR JSON schema

### Types to Add JSON Support
- ModuleDefinition[TA, VA]
- ModuleDefinitionType[TA]
- ModuleDefinitionValue[TA, VA]
- TypeDefinition variants
- ValueDefinition
- Type variants (TypeReference, TypeRecord, etc.)
- Name, FQName, Path

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] json.Marshal(module) works without ad-hoc conversion
- [ ] Support full distribution emission
- [ ] Support JSONL split emission
- [ ] Support metadata lines in JSONL
- [ ] Round-trip: Unmarshal matches original
- [ ] Tests for all emission strategies

title: Improve validation performance for large Morphir IR JSON files
description:
The morphir validate command hangs indefinitely when processing large Morphir IR JSON files.

## Problem
Validation performance degrades dramatically with file size:
- 99 byte minimal IR (base-ir.json): validates instantly ✓
- 71KB test IR (expected-morphir-ir.json): hangs indefinitely (timeout after 10s)
- 15MB production IR (docs/server/morphir-ir.json): hangs indefinitely

The issue occurs at compiledSchema.Validate(irData) in pkg/tooling/validation/validation.go:110, suggesting O(n²) or worse algorithmic complexity in the JSON schema validation library.

## Impact
- Users cannot validate real-world Morphir IR files
- TUI feature (--tui flag) is untestable with actual production data
- Blocks adoption of new interactive validation features
- BDD tests only work with minimal fixtures

## Test Cases
Working (instant):
- morphir validate tests/bdd/testdata/morphir-elm/cli-test-ir/base-ir.json

Hanging:
- morphir validate morphir-elm/tests-integration/cli/test-data/rentals/expected-morphir-ir.json
- morphir validate docs/server/morphir-ir.json

## Potential Solutions
1. Profile validation to identify bottleneck
2. Implement streaming/incremental JSON validation
3. Add validation caching for repeated validations
4. Evaluate alternative JSON schema validation libraries
5. Add timeout with progress indicators
6. Implement partial validation mode (structure only)
7. Consider lazy validation strategies

## Related
Discovered while testing TUI enhancements (line numbers, goto-line, auto-select)

title: Render markdown output with glamour for beautiful terminal display
description:
Enhance the existing markdown report output by rendering it beautifully in the terminal, similar to Charmbracelet's Glow CLI.

## Reference
- Glow CLI: https://github.com/charmbracelet/glow
- Glamour library (used by Glow): https://github.com/charmbracelet/glamour

## Current State
- `morphir validate --report markdown` outputs raw markdown text
- Users must pipe to external tools like `glow` or `bat` for nice rendering

## Desired State
- Automatically render markdown with glamour (the library Glow uses) when outputting to a terminal (TTY)
- Fall back to raw markdown when piped or redirected to a file
- Support `--no-color` flag to disable styling
- Achieve Glow-like beautiful rendering inline

## Implementation
```go
import "github.com/charmbracelet/glamour"

func renderMarkdown(content string) string {
    if \!isTerminal(os.Stdout) {
        return content // Raw markdown for pipes/files
    }
    
    renderer, _ := glamour.NewTermRenderer(
        glamour.WithAutoStyle(),
        glamour.WithWordWrap(terminalWidth()),
    )
    out, _ := renderer.Render(content)
    return out
}
```

## Features
- Auto-detect terminal vs pipe output
- Respect `NO_COLOR` environment variable
- Word wrap to terminal width
- Syntax highlighting for JSON code blocks (like Glow does)
- Styled tables, headers, and emphasis

## Example
```bash
# Beautiful Glow-like rendered output in terminal
morphir validate ./ir.json --report markdown

# Raw markdown when piped
morphir validate ./ir.json --report markdown > report.md
morphir validate ./ir.json --report markdown | less
```

## Libraries
- `github.com/charmbracelet/glamour` - Markdown rendering (same library Glow uses)
- `github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss` - Styling
- `github.com/mattn/go-isatty` - TTY detection

title: Add TUI validate command with interactive markdown viewer
description:
Create an interactive TUI version of the validate command using Charmbracelet libraries.

## Overview
Add a `--tui` or `-i` flag to the validate command that launches an interactive terminal UI for exploring validation results.

## UI Layout
```
┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Files           │ # Morphir IR Validation Report           │
│ ────────────    │                                          │
│ ▼ Validated     │ ❌ **Overall Status: ERRORS FOUND**      │
│   ├ base.json ✓ │                                          │
│   ├ list.json ✗ │ ## File: list.json                       │
│   └ tree.json ✗ │                                          │
│                 │ ### Error Analysis                       │
│                 │ ...                                       │
│                 │                                          │
│                 │ [j/k: scroll] [q: quit] [/: search]      │
└─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Features
- **Sidebar**: Treeview file explorer showing validated IR files
  - Flat tree for single files, expandable for multiple
  - Status indicators (✓/✗) for each file
  - Click/enter to select and view file's report
- **Main Content**: Rendered markdown report
  - Styled using glamour (Charmbracelet's markdown renderer)
  - Pager-like scrolling behavior (less/bat style)
  - Vim keybindings (j/k, gg/G, Ctrl+d/u, /)
- **Search**: Filter/search within report content
- **Keyboard navigation**: Full vim-style navigation

## Libraries
- `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea` - TUI framework
- `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles` - UI components (viewport, list)
- `github.com/charmbracelet/glamour` - Markdown rendering
- `github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss` - Styling

## Usage
```bash
morphir validate ./path/to/ir --tui
morphir validate ./file1.json ./file2.json --tui
```

## Dependencies
- Depends on: morphir-go-y4a (reusable TUI component)
- Related: morphir-go-z3b (glow-style markdown output)

title: Add error code appendix to validation reports
description:
Improve validation report readability by adding an appendix with indexed rule descriptions.

## Current State
- Validation errors repeat similar explanations for each occurrence
- Users see the same suggestion text multiple times in long reports

## Desired State
- Assign error codes to each violation type (e.g., E001: Pattern mismatch, E002: oneOf failed)
- Reference error codes inline in the Detailed Errors section
- Add an Appendix section at the end with full descriptions for each error code used
- Only include error codes that appear in the report (no unused codes)

## Example Output
```markdown
### Detailed Errors

**Path:** `/distribution/3/modules/0/0/1/2`
**Issue:** [E001] '2052' does not match pattern...

---

## Appendix: Error Code Reference

### E001: Pattern Mismatch
Each name part must be either a lowercase word (starting with a letter) or a standalone number.
The Morphir IR schema requires identifiers to follow specific naming conventions.

### E002: Type Variant Mismatch
The value doesn't match any of the expected type variants...
```

## Benefits
- Reduces report verbosity
- Easier to scan for specific error types
- Consistent error documentation
close_reason: Implemented error code appendix with inline codes and appendix section

title: Design workspace member configuration schema
description:
Design the TOML schema for declaring workspace members. Include:
- [workspace.members] array with glob patterns (e.g., 'packages/*', 'libs/**')
- [project] section for member projects with name, version, exposedModules
- Consider exclude patterns for ignoring directories
- Document relationship between workspace root config and member configs
design:
# Workspace Members Configuration Schema

## Overview

This design follows patterns from Cargo and npm workspaces, adapted for Morphir's needs.

## 1. Workspace Root Configuration (morphir.toml)

```toml
[morphir]
version = "^3.0.0"

[workspace]
# Existing fields
root = ""
output_dir = ".morphir"

# NEW: Member discovery via glob patterns
members = [
    "packages/*",           # All direct subdirs of packages/
    "libs/**",              # Recursive: all subdirs under libs/
    "apps/*/frontend",      # Nested pattern
]

# NEW: Exclude specific paths from member discovery
exclude = [
    "packages/deprecated",
    "**/testdata",
]

# NEW: Default member to use when none specified (optional)
default_member = "packages/core"

# NEW: Shared configuration inherited by all members
[workspace.defaults]
source_directory = "src"
```

## 2. Project Section (for member projects)

Member projects use a `[project]` section in their morphir.toml:

```toml
# packages/core/morphir.toml

[project]
# Required: Project name - flexible format
# Can be any valid identifier: "my-project", "MyProject", "Morphir.Core"
name = "morphir-core"

# Optional: Package version (can inherit from workspace)
version = "1.0.0"

# Required: Directory containing source files (relative to project root)
source_directory = "src"

# Required: Modules exposed in the public API
exposed_modules = [
    "Types",
    "SDK",
    "IR",
]

# Optional: Module prefix for Elm-style qualified names
# If not set, derived from name or inferred from source structure
# Use this for morphir-elm compatibility or explicit module namespacing
module_prefix = "Morphir.Core"

# Optional: Dependencies on other workspace members
# dependencies = ["morphir-sdk"]
```

### Field Descriptions

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | string | Yes | Project identifier (flexible: kebab-case, PascalCase, dot-separated, etc.) |
| `version` | string | No | Semantic version, can use `workspace = true` to inherit |
| `source_directory` | string | Yes | Source code location relative to project root |
| `exposed_modules` | []string | Yes | Public modules (without module_prefix) |
| `module_prefix` | string | No | Elm-style module prefix for qualified names (defaults to name if valid, otherwise derived) |

### Name vs Module Prefix

- **name**: Project identifier used for references, dependencies, and tooling. Flexible format.
- **module_prefix**: Elm-style dotted prefix for module qualification. Used when generating IR or for morphir-elm compatibility.

Examples:
```toml
# Modern style - explicit separation
name = "my-awesome-lib"
module_prefix = "MyAwesome.Lib"

# Elm-compatible style - name doubles as prefix
name = "Morphir.SDK"
# module_prefix defaults to "Morphir.SDK" (valid Elm module name)

# Simple project - auto-derived prefix
name = "utils"
# module_prefix defaults to "Utils" (PascalCase conversion)
```

## 3. morphir.json Compatibility (finos/morphir-elm)

The classic morphir.json format is automatically detected and mapped:

```json
{
    "name": "My.Package",
    "sourceDirectory": "src",
    "exposedModules": ["Foo", "Bar"]
}
```

### Mapping to [project] Section

| morphir.json | morphir.toml [project] |
|--------------|------------------------|
| `name` | `name` AND `module_prefix` (same value, since morphir.json names are always Elm-style) |
| `sourceDirectory` | `source_directory` |
| `exposedModules` | `exposed_modules` |

### Detection Priority

1. `morphir.toml` (preferred)
2. `.morphir/morphir.toml`  
3. `morphir.json` (legacy compatibility)

## 4. Workspace Types

### Virtual Workspace (no root project)

```toml
# Root morphir.toml - workspace only, no project
[workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]
```

### Root Package Workspace (workspace + project)

```toml
# Root morphir.toml - both workspace and project
[workspace]
members = ["libs/*"]

[project]
name = "my-app"
module_prefix = "MyApp"
source_directory = "src"
exposed_modules = ["Main"]
```

## 5. Directory Structure Examples

### Multi-package Workspace

```
my-workspace/
├── morphir.toml              # [workspace] with members
├── packages/
│   ├── core/
│   │   ├── morphir.toml      # [project] section
│   │   └── src/
│   ├── sdk/
│   │   ├── morphir.toml
│   │   └── src/
│   └── deprecated/           # Excluded
│       └── morphir.toml
└── libs/
    └── utils/
        ├── morphir.json      # Legacy format supported
        └── src/
```

### Hybrid with Root Project

```
my-app/
├── morphir.toml              # [workspace] + [project]
├── src/                      # Root project sources
└── libs/
    ├── internal/
    │   └── morphir.toml
    └── shared/
        └── morphir.json
```

## 6. Glob Pattern Specification

Patterns follow Go's `filepath.Match` plus `**` for recursive matching:

| Pattern | Matches |
|---------|---------|
| `*` | Any single path segment |
| `**` | Zero or more path segments (recursive) |
| `?` | Any single character |
| `[abc]` | Character class |

Examples:
- `packages/*` → `packages/foo`, `packages/bar` (not `packages/foo/bar`)
- `libs/**` → `libs/a`, `libs/a/b`, `libs/a/b/c`
- `apps/*/frontend` → `apps/web/frontend`, `apps/mobile/frontend`

## 7. Module Prefix Derivation

When `module_prefix` is not explicitly set:

1. If `name` is a valid Elm module name (PascalCase, dot-separated), use it directly
2. Otherwise, convert `name` to PascalCase:
   - `my-project` → `MyProject`
   - `foo_bar` → `FooBar`
   - `utils` → `Utils`

This ensures backward compatibility with morphir-elm while allowing modern naming conventions.

## 8. Config Resolution

When loading a workspace:

1. Find workspace root (walk up looking for morphir.toml with [workspace])
2. Resolve member globs against workspace root
3. Apply exclude patterns
4. For each matched directory:
   a. Look for morphir.toml with [project]
   b. Fall back to .morphir/morphir.toml
   c. Fall back to morphir.json
5. Derive module_prefix if not set
6. Merge workspace.defaults into each project
7. Return Workspace with resolved []Project

title: Sync GitHub Actions workflows with just recipes
description:
Our GitHub Actions CI workflows are not using our just recipes, which makes it harder to test CI locally. We should refactor the workflows to use just commands so that:

1. Developers can run `just ci-check` locally and get the same results as CI
2. There's a single source of truth for build/test/lint commands
3. Workflow maintenance is simplified - changes to build logic only need to happen in the Justfile

## Current State
- CI workflows define their own commands inline
- `Justfile` has `ci-check`, `lint`, `test`, `fmt`, etc. recipes
- The two are not always in sync

## Desired State
- CI workflows call `just` commands instead of inline scripts
- Local `just ci-check` produces equivalent results to CI
- All build logic lives in the Justfile

## Tasks
- [ ] Audit current CI workflow commands vs just recipes
- [ ] Update CI workflows to use just recipes
- [ ] Verify CI passes with the new approach
- [ ] Document the change in README
close_reason: Completed in PR #15 (e0de1e9). All GitHub Actions workflows now use just recipes (fmt-check, lint, test, build, verify). Removed duplicate ci-check scripts and ensured CI/local development use the same build logic.

Native-only operations must refuse explicitly on unsupported targets while keeping portable help/inspection usable. New/touched automation uses MoonBit .mbtx. Ion is preferred; Morphir JSON remains supported with checked loss boundaries; IR 4.0.0 remains draft. Logs default under .morphir/logs and honor explicit paths. Include focused real CLI acceptance, failure/cleanup tests and meaningful cross-platform evidence. Preserve existing run/workspace/execute/verify/conform/toolchain interfaces. Coordinate the small shared command-registration edits; keep lane implementation in separate modules. Existing open integration/numeric/UI tasks are related unless a concrete dependency is listed. Merge, release, publishing and production cutover still need applicable maintainer authorization.
Optional authenticated-provider/profile work. 2026-10-17 maintainer correction: prioritize an extensible tooling ecosystem analogous to LSP/BSP. Baseline flow is advertised publisher/author and capability descriptions -> explicit user/host selection -> compatible interface/feature negotiation -> useful operation and diagnostics. Authorship assertions, user approval, capability compatibility, model validation and cryptographically authenticated provenance are separate concepts. A user's approval need not depend on a signed registry or repeated runtime publisher authentication. Do not represent self-declared authorship as verified identity.

MEP describes shared operations/data/lifecycle independently of binding/runtime.
